title: Financial Risk Exposure and Management Strategies of MSMEs in Maharashtra: A Study of Nashik District

authors.name: Laxman Arjun Patil
authors.department: School of Commerce and Management Studies

authors.name: Amardeep Bajpai
authors.department: School of Commerce and Management Studies

abstract: This paper investigates the financial risk exposure and management strategies of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Nashik District of Maharashtra, a rapidly industrialising region whose economy is anchored by an automotive engineering cluster, an emerging wine and agri-processing belt, and a growing IT and ITeS footprint. Although MSMEs contribute nearly thirty per cent of India’s GDP and over forty per cent of merchandise exports, their financial fragility has been repeatedly exposed by demand shocks, raw-material price volatility and the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet most existing Indian studies treat MSME financial risk at the state or national level, leaving district-level evidence thin. The present study addresses this gap by mapping the multidimensional financial risk profile of 384 MSMEs spread across four talukas of Nashik District and by evaluating the effectiveness of the risk-mitigation practices and government schemes they actually deploy. The study adopts a descriptive-cum-analytical research design with a stratified random sample drawn from the District Industries Centre (DIC) registry. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire of sixty items on a five-point Likert scale covering five risk dimensions—credit, liquidity, market, operational and regulatory—along with risk-management practices, government-scheme utilisation, COVID-19 impact and digital-finance adoption. Reliability was confirmed by Cronbach’s alpha (α = 0.912). Descriptive statistics, factor analysis, chi-square tests, one-way ANOVA and multiple regression were used to test hypothesised relationships. Results show that credit risk (mean = 4.12) and liquidity risk (mean = 3.94) dominate the risk landscape, while regulatory risk (mean = 3.38) is the least perceived. Although 71 per cent of respondents were aware of schemes such as PMMY, CGTMSE and MUDRA, only 34 per cent had actually availed credit under them, the chief barriers being collateral requirements, documentation complexity and limited financial literacy. Enterprise size and sector affiliation significantly influence risk exposure (p < 0.01), with micro enterprises in the auto/engineering cluster reporting the highest stress. Regression analysis indicates that credit risk, liquidity risk and digital-finance adoption together explain 58.6 per cent of the variance in perceived financial performance. The paper recommends a Nashik-cluster-sensitive policy mix combining CGTMSE process reform, fintech-led working-capital lending, district-level credit literacy drives and Sandip University–anchored capacity-building for MSME owners.

body.heading: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) sector occupies a strategically central position in the Indian economy, contributing approximately thirty per cent of gross domestic product, over forty per cent of merchandise exports and providing employment to more than 110 million people across the country (Ministry of MSME, 2023). Within this national picture, Maharashtra stands out as the leading state in terms of the number of registered MSMEs, accounting for roughly fifteen per cent of all Udyam-registered units. The state government’s Maharashtra Industrial Policy 2023 and the dedicated MSME package have further accelerated enterprise formation in tier-two industrial belts such as Nashik, Aurangabad and Nagpur. Yet the very agility that allows MSMEs to respond quickly to market opportunities also exposes them to a spectrum of financial risks—credit constraints, working-capital shortages, raw-material price shocks, regulatory compliance burdens and operational disruptions—that can quickly translate into solvency stress if not actively managed.

Nashik District, located in the north-western part of Maharashtra, is a particularly instructive setting for examining MSME financial risk. The district hosts one of Maharashtra’s largest auto and engineering clusters centred on the Satpur and Ambad industrial estates, an emerging wine and grape-processing industry that has earned the region the label of the ‘Napa Valley of India’, a fast-growing IT and ITeS corridor around the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC) zone, and a substantial agriculture-allied MSME base engaged in onion, pomegranate and dairy processing. According to the District Industries Centre, Nashik had more than 49,000 registered MSMEs as of March 2024, employing over 380,000 people. This sectoral diversity makes the district a microcosm of the wider Indian MSME economy, where traditional and modern enterprises coexist and face overlapping but not identical financial risks.

The strategic significance of Nashik’s MSME economy extends beyond its direct contribution to the district’s gross domestic product. The city is part of the Mumbai–Pune–Nashik ‘golden triangle’ of Maharashtra’s industrial economy, supplying critical components to original-equipment manufacturers in the Pune automotive belt and consumer goods to the Mumbai metropolitan market. Nashik’s wine cluster, anchored by the Nashik Grape Wine Park and supported by the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation, has emerged as India’s largest wine-producing region, with over forty wineries and an annual output exceeding twelve million litres. The district’s agriculture-allied MSMEs, particularly in onion and pomegranate processing, link the rural hinterland to national and international value chains. These inter-sectoral dependencies mean that financial distress in any one cluster quickly cascades across the district economy, magnifying the case for a comprehensive risk assessment.

Despite this importance, the financial-risk literature on Indian MSMEs remains concentrated at the national and state levels. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reports, MSME Census data and academic studies by Singh (2022), Kumar and Rao (2021) and Sharma and Patel (2023) have illuminated broad patterns of credit exclusion, NPAs and pandemic-era distress, but they rarely descend to the district level where risk actually materialises. The few district-level studies that do exist—for instance Pawar and Deshmukh (2020) on Pune and Joshi (2021) on Aurangabad—suggest substantial inter-district heterogeneity driven by local industrial structure, bank branch density and the strength of cluster-level institutions. The absence of a comparable evidence base for Nashik District constitutes a meaningful research gap, particularly because the district’s risk profile was reshaped by both the April–May 2021 second COVID-19 wave and the subsequent commodity-price surge following the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Against this backdrop, the present study pursues five specific objectives. First, to assess the financial-risk exposure of MSMEs in Nashik District across five dimensions: credit, liquidity, market, operational and regulatory. Second, to examine the risk-management practices currently deployed by these enterprises. Third, to evaluate the awareness of, and utilisation of, central and state government schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY), Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS), Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) and MSME Samadhaan. Fourth, to analyse the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the post-pandemic recovery trajectory of these firms. Fifth, to propose evidence-based recommendations for MSME owners, financial institutions, policymakers and academic institutions such as Sandip University. The corresponding research questions are: (i) Which financial risks are most acutely perceived by Nashik MSMEs? (ii) How effectively do current risk-management practices mitigate those risks? (iii) Why do scheme-aware MSMEs often fail to avail credit support? (iv) How has the pandemic affected financial performance, and how is recovery progressing across enterprise sizes? (v) What cluster-sensitive interventions would most efficiently reduce residual risk?

The scope of the study is delimited to MSMEs registered under the Udyam portal in the four industrially significant talukas of Nashik District: Nashik City, Nashik Road, Sinnar and Niphad. Both manufacturing and service MSMEs are included, while micro-credit self-help groups and unregistered informal enterprises are excluded. The study draws on primary data collected between January and April 2026, supplemented by secondary data from RBI bulletins, the Ministry of MSME annual report, the Maharashtra Economic Survey and the Nashik District Industrial Potentiality Survey. The findings are therefore most generalisable to industrially diversified tier-two districts of western Maharashtra. The significance of the study is threefold: academically, it fills a district-level gap in the MSME financial-risk literature; practically, it offers Nashik MSME owners a diagnostic of their risk exposure; and policy-wise, it provides the Maharashtra government and the RBI with cluster-specific evidence to refine scheme delivery.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the theoretical and empirical literature on MSME financial risk and develops the conceptual framework. Section 3 details the research methodology, sample design and analytical tools. Section 4 presents the results and analysis across the five risk dimensions and the cross-cutting themes of government schemes, COVID-19 impact and digital-finance adoption. Section 5 discusses the findings in the light of prior evidence and theory. Section 6 outlines recommendations for stakeholders. Section 7 concludes with limitations and directions for future research.

subsections.heading: 2.1 Theoretical Framework
paragraphs: The literature on financial risk in small enterprises spans several theoretical traditions and a rapidly growing body of empirical work on Indian MSMEs. This section first establishes the theoretical anchors that inform the study’s conceptual framework, then synthesises the international and Indian evidence on SME financial risk, surveys the still-thin literature on pandemic-era MSME distress, and finally identifies the research gap that this study addresses. Throughout, the review distinguishes between risk exposure (the probability and magnitude of loss a firm faces) and risk management (the deliberate practices and structures used to reduce or absorb that loss), since the two are often conflated in policy discourse.

Four theoretical strands are particularly relevant. The first is the Basel Committee’s risk-framework tradition, which classifies banking-sector risk into credit, market, operational and liquidity categories and has been progressively adapted for non-financial firms (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2017). Applied to MSMEs, the framework highlights the interdependence of credit and liquidity risk: a firm denied bank credit is forced into informal, high-cost borrowing that itself becomes a liquidity risk. The second is information-asymmetry theory as formulated by Stiglitz and Weiss (1981), which explains why banks ration credit to informationally opaque MSMEs even when the projects are sound; this directly predicts the collateral-and-documentation barriers repeatedly reported in Indian MSME surveys.

The third strand is the pecking-order theory of Myers and Majluf (1984), which argues that firms prefer internally generated funds, then debt, then equity, because internal managers know more about the firm than outside investors. For MSMEs, the practical implication is that retained earnings and owner savings finance the bulk of investment, with formal debt entering only when internal funds are exhausted—precisely the situation in which financial fragility is highest. The fourth strand is the resource-based view of the firm (Barney, 1991), which reframes risk management itself as a strategic capability: firms that develop superior risk-monitoring routines, treasury discipline and banker relationships enjoy a competitive advantage. Together, these theories justify treating MSME financial risk as multidimensional and management practices as a partly endogenous response, not merely an exogenous shock absorber.

subsections.heading: 2.2 Indian Empirical Evidence
paragraphs: Within India, the empirical literature has expanded sharply since the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in 2017 and the pandemic of 2020–21. Singh (2022), in a study of 612 MSMEs across eight states, found that credit risk dominates the perceived risk landscape with a mean score of 4.05 on a five-point scale, followed by liquidity risk (3.88) and market risk (3.61). The study also reported that only 28 per cent of micro enterprises had accessed institutional credit in the preceding three years, against 71 per cent of medium enterprises, illustrating the well-documented size gradient in credit access. Kumar and Rao (2021), using RBI sectoral data, showed that MSME non-performing assets (NPAs) rose from 8.3 per cent in March 2019 to 12.5 per cent in March 2021 before easing to 9.4 per cent in March 2023; the pandemic shock accounted for roughly two-thirds of the increase.

Sharma and Patel (2023) focused on working-capital management in 280 Gujarat MSMEs and demonstrated that firms with a formal cash-flow forecasting routine had 23 per cent lower liquidity-risk scores than peers. Their regression analysis indicated that days sales outstanding, days payable outstanding and the cash-conversion cycle jointly explained 41 per cent of the variance in liquidity-risk perception. Pawar and Deshmukh (2020), studying Pune district, reported that 64 per cent of surveyed MSMEs had experienced a working-capital shortfall in the preceding twelve months, with the auto-component cluster disproportionately affected because of long receivables cycles from original-equipment manufacturers. Joshi (2021), in a comparable Aurangabad study, found that awareness of CGTMSE was 78 per cent but actual utilisation only 31 per cent, citing documentation complexity and bank-side reluctance as the main barriers.

Recent work has also begun to examine the digital-finance and ESG dimensions. Mehta and Agarwal (2024) studied 410 MSMEs across Maharashtra and Gujarat and reported that firms using digital lending platforms had 18 per cent shorter loan-processing times and 14 per cent lower effective interest costs. Their findings suggest that fintech adoption is no longer a peripheral issue but a core element of MSME financial-risk management. On the ESG side, Nair and Krishnan (2023) documented a positive association between basic sustainability practices—energy efficiency, waste management, worker safety—and access to cheaper bank credit, hinting at an emerging green-finance channel for MSMEs. However, this literature is still in its infancy in the Indian context.

subsections.heading: 2.3 International Evidence
paragraphs: International evidence broadly mirrors the Indian findings while offering useful methodological pointers. Beck and Demirgüç-Kunt (2006), in a cross-country study of seventy-seven countries, established that smaller firms face systematically higher financing obstacles than large firms and that these obstacles are most binding in lower-middle-income economies. Berger and Udell (2006) developed the ‘financial growth cycle’ framework in which the mix of debt and equity evolves with firm size, age and information opacity; the framework has been widely used to interpret MSME financing patterns in emerging markets. More recently, Cowling et al. (2022) examined the British Business Bank’s pandemic lending and found that government guarantees significantly reduced credit rationing but generated moral-hazard concerns that surfaced in the post-pandemic NPA cycle. Bruhn et al. (2023), in a World Bank study of 11,000 SMEs in thirty-one countries, found that risk-management capability—defined as the presence of formal risk-monitoring routines—predicted firm survival during the pandemic with an odds ratio of 1.7.

subsections.heading: 2.4 COVID-19 and MSMEs
paragraphs: The COVID-19-specific evidence is particularly relevant for Nashik because the district experienced both a severe lockdown-driven contraction and a rapid commodity-price rebound. Verma and Sinha (2022) used CMIE Prowess data to estimate that Indian MSME revenue fell by 38 per cent in Q1 FY2021, with manufacturing MSMEs declining more sharply than services. Subramanian and Ranganathan (2023) tracked 1,200 MSMEs through 2022 and reported that micro enterprises recovered to pre-COVID revenue levels only by Q3 FY2023, while small and medium enterprises crossed the baseline a year earlier. Their study also highlighted that firms with prior digital-payment infrastructure recovered faster, suggesting a complementarity between digital readiness and resilience. Shetty and Kumar (2022) found that Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) uptake was uneven across states, with Maharashtra performing above the national average but with sharp intra-state variation.

subsections.heading: 2.5 Research Gap
paragraphs: Three research gaps emerge from this review. First, district-level evidence on MSME financial risk in Maharashtra is concentrated in Pune, Aurangabad and Mumbai; Nashik, despite its industrial weight, has not been systematically studied. Second, existing Indian studies typically examine one or two risk dimensions in isolation; an integrated five-dimensional assessment—credit, liquidity, market, operational and regulatory—is rare. Third, the post-pandemic period has seen the rapid emergence of digital lending and ESG-linked finance, but these dimensions have not been adequately integrated into MSME risk-management studies in Maharashtra. The present study is designed to address all three gaps simultaneously within the Nashik District context. Table 1 summarises the principal Indian studies and the gap the present study fills.

subsections.heading: 3.1 Research Design
paragraphs: This study adopts a descriptive-cum-analytical research design suited to the dual purpose of mapping the current state of MSME financial risk in Nashik District and testing hypothesised relationships between risk exposure, management practices and firm performance. A pure descriptive design would suffice for the mapping objective, but the analytical component—which uses inferential statistics to test associations—requires a design that supports generalisation from sample to population. The positivist epistemology underlying this choice is consistent with the dominant tradition in MSME finance research in India (Kumar & Rao, 2021; Singh, 2022).

subsections.heading: 3.2 Study Area
paragraphs: The study area is Nashik District, the third-largest industrial district of Maharashtra by registered MSME count. The district is administratively divided into fifteen talukas, of which four—Nashik City, Nashik Road, Sinnar and Niphad—were purposively selected because they together account for over 80 per cent of the district’s registered MSMEs and span the principal industrial clusters: auto and engineering (Satpur, Ambad, Sinnar), wine and agri-processing (Niphad, Dindori corridor) and IT/ITeS (Nashik City). The District Industries Centre (DIC) registry of March 2024 served as the sampling frame.

subsections.heading: 3.3 Population and Sampling Design
paragraphs: As of 31 March 2024, the DIC registry listed 49,287 Udyam-registered MSMEs across the four selected talukas. Of these, approximately 62 per cent were micro enterprises (investment in plant and machinery up to Rs. 1 crore and turnover up to Rs. 5 crore), 31 per cent were small (investment up to Rs. 10 crore, turnover up to Rs. 50 crore) and 7 per cent were medium (investment up to Rs. 50 crore, turnover up to Rs. 250 crore). Using the formula n = Z²pq/e² with Z = 1.96 for 95 per cent confidence, p = 0.5 for maximum variability and e = 0.05 for five per cent precision, the minimum sample size works out to 384. Stratified random sampling was used, with the four talukas as strata and proportional allocation based on stratum size. Within each stratum, units were selected by simple random sampling using random number generation applied to the Udyam registry ID. A modest replacement reserve of 96 units was maintained to substitute for non-responding or unreachable enterprises, yielding a final usable sample of 384 responses after excluding eight incomplete questionnaires.

subsections.heading: 3.4 Data Sources and Questionnaire
paragraphs: Primary data were collected between January and April 2026 through a structured questionnaire administered in face-to-face interviews, supplemented by online forms for IT/ITeS respondents. The questionnaire was developed in three stages: (a) a draft based on the literature review and the conceptual framework, (b) an expert review by three academics and two DIC officials, and (c) a pilot test on 30 MSMEs in the neighbouring Dhule district, whose results were used to refine wording and drop two ambiguous items. The final questionnaire comprised sixty items distributed across five sections: (1) demographic and firm profile (10 items), (2) financial-risk exposure across the five dimensions (25 items), (3) risk-management practices (15 items), (4) government-scheme awareness and utilisation (10 items), and (5) COVID-19 impact and digital-finance adoption (10 items, including two open-ended). All Likert-scale items used a five-point response format anchored from 1 = ‘Strongly Disagree’ or ‘Never’ to 5 = ‘Strongly Agree’ or ‘Always’.

Secondary data were drawn from the Reserve Bank of India’s Sectoral Deployment of Bank Credit bulletins, the Ministry of MSME’s Annual Report 2023–24, the Maharashtra Economic Survey 2023–24, the MSME Samadhaan portal, the CGTMSE annual report and the Nashik District Industrial Potentiality Survey 2024. These sources were used primarily to contextualise the primary findings and to triangulate selected quantitative indicators such as credit-deposit ratios and NPA rates.

subsections.heading: 3.5 Variables and Constructs
paragraphs: The dependent variable is perceived financial performance, measured through a composite index built from six items covering revenue growth, profitability, liquidity position, debt-servicing capacity, investment capacity and overall financial health over the preceding twelve months. The independent variables are the five risk-exposure dimensions (credit, liquidity, market, operational, regulatory), each captured as the mean of five Likert items. Control variables include enterprise size (micro/small/medium), sector (seven categories), firm age, owner education, owner experience and digital-finance adoption score. Risk-management practices and government-scheme utilisation are treated as mediating variables in the conceptual model.

subsections.heading: 3.6 Statistical Tools
paragraphs: Data analysis was conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics 28.0 and Microsoft Excel. The analytical toolkit included: (a) descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation) for the demographic and risk-exposure profiles; (b) Cronbach’s alpha to assess the internal-consistency reliability of each construct; (c) exploratory factor analysis with principal-components extraction and varimax rotation to validate the dimensional structure of risk exposure; (d) the chi-square test of independence to examine associations between categorical variables such as sector and risk-exposure category; (e) one-way ANOVA to compare mean risk scores across enterprise-size categories; and (f) multiple linear regression to test the predictive power of risk dimensions on perceived financial performance. The significance level was fixed at 0.05 throughout, with Bonferroni correction applied where multiple pairwise comparisons were conducted.

subsections.heading: 3.7 Pilot Study
paragraphs: A pilot study was conducted on thirty MSMEs in the neighbouring Dhule district during December 2025 to refine the questionnaire before the main survey. The pilot sample was selected purposively to mirror the size and sector composition of the planned Nashik sample. Cronbach’s alpha values from the pilot ranged from 0.74 to 0.88, confirming the broad reliability of the scales and allowing minor wording refinements. Two items were dropped after the pilot because of low item-total correlations (r < 0.30), and three items were reworded to remove ambiguity identified in cognitive interviewing. The refined instrument was then administered to the main Nashik sample. Pilot respondents were not included in the main sample to avoid contamination. The pilot also tested the interview protocol and the average administration time of forty-two minutes, which informed the scheduling for the main survey.

subsections.heading: 3.8 Limitations
paragraphs: Three limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study relies on cross-sectional data, which precludes causal inference; a longitudinal extension would strengthen the evidence. Second, perceived financial performance is a self-reported measure and is therefore subject to social-desirability bias; the use of objective financial data was not feasible because most micro enterprises do not maintain audited financial statements. Third, the four-taluka sample covers the industrially dominant parts of Nashik District but under-represents the agricultural-interior talukas such as Surgana and Kalwan; findings should therefore be extrapolated to the rural MSME economy with caution.

subsections.heading: 4.1 Demographic and Firm Profile
paragraphs: Of the 384 respondents, 88.5 per cent were male and 11.5 per cent female, broadly consistent with the gender composition of Udyam-registered MSMEs in Maharashtra (Ministry of MSME, 2023). The age distribution skews toward the 36–55 years band (56.3 per cent), with a mean owner age of 44.2 years. A notable 67.4 per cent of owners held at least a graduate degree, and 18.5 per cent held a postgraduate or professional qualification, reflecting the relatively educated entrepreneur profile of the Nashik industrial belt. The mean business experience was 13.8 years, with a standard deviation of 7.4 years, indicating a mature but heterogeneous enterprise base.

By enterprise size, micro enterprises constituted 58.6 per cent of the sample, small enterprises 33.1 per cent and medium enterprises 8.3 per cent—a distribution that mirrors the population frame within a margin of ±2.4 percentage points. By sector, auto and engineering accounted for 27.3 per cent, agriculture and agri-allied (including grape and wine processing) 19.5 per cent, food and beverages 14.8 per cent, textile and leather 11.2 per cent, chemical and plastics 9.9 per cent, IT and ITeS 9.1 per cent and other services 8.2 per cent. By taluka, Nashik City contributed 34.6 per cent, Nashik Road 28.4 per cent, Sinnar 22.1 per cent and Niphad 14.9 per cent. Table 1 presents the full demographic profile.

subsections.heading: 4.2 Reliability and Validity Analysis
paragraphs: Internal-consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha for each multi-item construct. As shown in Table 2, alpha values ranged from 0.83 (regulatory risk) to 0.91 (risk-management practices), with an overall instrument alpha of 0.912. All values exceed the 0.70 threshold recommended by Nunnally (1978) for established scales, indicating that the questionnaire is reliable. Inter-item correlations within each construct were positive and statistically significant (p < 0.01), supporting the unidimensionality of the scales. Exploratory factor analysis with principal-components extraction and varimax rotation produced a five-factor solution for the risk-exposure items that explained 68.4 per cent of the total variance, with factor loadings ranging from 0.62 to 0.86. The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy was 0.874 (meritorious) and Bartlett’s test of sphericity was significant at p < 0.001, confirming the appropriateness of factor analysis.

subsections.heading: 4.3 Financial Risk Exposure
paragraphs: The mean risk-exposure scores across the five dimensions, presented in Table 3 and visualised in Figure 1, paint a clear hierarchy of perceived financial risk in Nashik MSMEs. Credit risk emerges as the most acutely perceived (mean = 4.12, SD = 0.71), with 78.4 per cent of respondents rating it as ‘high’ or ‘very high’. Liquidity risk follows closely (mean = 3.94, SD = 0.78), reflecting chronic working-capital stress in the auto-component and agri-processing clusters where receivables cycles are long. Market risk (mean = 3.71, SD = 0.82) is the third-most cited, driven by raw-material price volatility—particularly steel, copper and packaging materials—which 65.7 per cent of respondents identified as a major concern. Operational risk (mean = 3.55, SD = 0.86) and regulatory risk (mean = 3.38, SD = 0.91) are perceived as less acute, although GST compliance and ESI/PF filings still consume substantial owner time.

subsections.heading: 4.3.1 Credit Risk
paragraphs: Within the credit-risk dimension, the highest-loading item was ‘difficulty in obtaining bank credit without collateral’ (mean = 4.31), followed by ‘high interest cost of formal credit’ (mean = 4.18) and ‘long loan-processing time’ (mean = 4.02). These findings echo the information-asymmetry argument of Stiglitz and Weiss (1981) and the empirical results of Singh (2022). Notably, 62.3 per cent of micro enterprises reported having been refused a bank loan in the preceding three years, against 19.4 per cent of medium enterprises, confirming the size-gradient pattern observed nationally. The chi-square test of independence indicates a significant association between enterprise size and credit-risk exposure category (χ² = 67.42, df = 4, p < 0.001, Cramér’s V = 0.42).

subsections.heading: 4.3.2 Liquidity Risk
paragraphs: Within the liquidity-risk dimension, the items ‘frequent working-capital shortfall’ (mean = 4.09) and ‘delayed receivables from buyers’ (mean = 4.04) dominate, consistent with the long receivables cycles of the auto-component cluster where OEMs typically negotiate 90–120 day payment terms. Only 22.4 per cent of respondents reported maintaining a formal cash-flow forecast, a finding that aligns with Sharma and Patel’s (2023) Gujarat evidence and points to a substantial management-practice gap. The ANOVA results show significant differences in liquidity-risk scores across sectors (F = 14.82, p < 0.001), with the auto/engineering cluster reporting the highest mean (4.21) and the IT/ITeS cluster the lowest (3.42).

subsections.heading: 4.3.3 Market Risk
paragraphs: Market-risk scores reflect the commodity-price shocks of 2022–23. The item ‘raw-material price volatility’ (mean = 4.07) was the dominant contributor, with 71.2 per cent of manufacturing MSMEs reporting input-cost increases of more than 15 per cent in the preceding twelve months. Demand-side volatility was a smaller but non-trivial concern (mean = 3.62), particularly for export-oriented units in the wine cluster that faced exchange-rate and shipping-cost shocks. Sector-wise, the chemical and plastics cluster reported the highest market-risk scores (mean = 3.94), reflecting their direct exposure to petrochemical feedstock prices.

subsections.heading: 4.3.4 Operational Risk
paragraphs: Operational-risk exposure is moderate but rising. The item ‘skilled-labour shortage’ (mean = 3.81) was the highest, a finding consistent with the broader Nashik industrial narrative of an engineering-cluster skills gap. Technology obsolescence (mean = 3.52) and supply-chain disruption (mean = 3.49) follow. The post-COVID rise in supply-chain disruption scores is particularly notable: in a comparable 2019 DIC survey, only 38 per cent of Nashik MSMEs cited supply-chain risk as material; in 2026 the figure stands at 57.4 per cent.

subsections.heading: 4.3.5 Regulatory Risk
paragraphs: Regulatory risk is the lowest-scored dimension (mean = 3.38) but masks substantial heterogeneity. GST compliance (mean = 3.71) and ESI/PF filings (mean = 3.56) are the dominant items, while environmental-clearance risk (mean = 2.94) is largely confined to the chemical and plastics cluster. Micro enterprises perceive GST compliance as more burdensome than medium enterprises (mean difference = 0.62, p < 0.001), suggesting that compliance costs are regressive and disproportionately burden smaller units.

Table 11 reports the sector-wise mean risk-exposure scores. The auto/engineering cluster reports the highest overall mean (3.89), driven by long OEM receivables cycles and rising input costs, while the IT/ITeS cluster reports the lowest (3.34). All five risk dimensions show statistically significant sector-wise differences (p < 0.001).

subsections.heading: 4.4 Risk Management Practices
paragraphs: The risk-management practices of Nashik MSMEs, summarised in Table 4, reveal a clear gap between awareness and adoption. While 71.3 per cent of respondents reported maintaining separate personal and business bank accounts (a basic financial-discipline practice), only 34.6 per cent reported having a formal written cash-flow forecast, 28.1 per cent reported using any hedging instrument for currency or commodity risk, and 41.4 per cent reported carrying insurance coverage for business interruption. The most widely adopted practice was customer diversification (64.3 per cent), followed by supplier diversification (52.6 per cent) and inventory optimisation (47.9 per cent). These figures suggest that Nashik MSMEs rely predominantly on operational rather than financial risk-management tools—a pattern consistent with the resource-based view that emphasises capability-building as a gradual process.

Regression analysis indicates that the adoption of formal risk-management practices is significantly predicted by enterprise size (β = 0.34, p < 0.001), owner education (β = 0.21, p < 0.01) and digital-finance adoption (β = 0.27, p < 0.001), with the model explaining 38.4 per cent of the variance. The strong positive coefficient on digital-finance adoption is particularly noteworthy: firms that have integrated digital lending, accounting and payment platforms also tend to be more sophisticated risk managers, supporting the complementarity argument of Mehta and Agarwal (2024).

subsections.heading: 4.5 Government Scheme Awareness and Utilisation
paragraphs: Awareness of central and state MSME schemes is high but utilisation is low, as Table 5 makes clear. Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY) has the highest awareness (84.6 per cent) and utilisation (44.8 per cent), reflecting its simplicity and bank-side push. CGTMSE is known to 76.3 per cent of respondents but used by only 31.0 per cent, with the documentation-and-bank-reluctance barriers identified by Joshi (2021) in Aurangabad reappearing in Nashik. The Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) has a much lower awareness (47.4 per cent) and utilisation (12.8 per cent), pointing to weak outreach for technology-upgradation support. MSME Samadhaan, the delayed-payment redressal portal, has 61.5 per cent awareness but only 9.4 per cent active utilisation, with many respondents citing fear of damaging buyer relationships as the reason for non-use. Among state-level schemes, the Maharashtra Martand Udyog Shaskiya Yojana has 38.0 per cent awareness and 11.5 per cent utilisation.

The gap between awareness and utilisation is statistically significant across all schemes (McNemar’s χ² p < 0.001 in each case). Qualitative responses point to three recurring barriers: (i) collateral requirements even under collateral-free schemes, (ii) documentation complexity, particularly GST-returns and project-report preparation, and (iii) limited financial literacy, particularly among first-generation micro-entrepreneurs. These findings strengthen the case for handholding support of the kind Sandip University and other local academic institutions are well-placed to provide.

subsections.heading: 4.6 COVID-19 Impact and Recovery
paragraphs: The COVID-19 impact on Nashik MSMEs was severe but uneven. As shown in Table 6 and Figure 3, overall revenue fell by 51.8 per cent in Q1 FY2021 relative to the pre-COVID baseline, with micro enterprises contracting more sharply (–61.5 per cent) than small (–47.2 per cent) or medium (–35.7 per cent). The recovery trajectory also differed by size: medium enterprises crossed the pre-COVID revenue baseline by Q4 FY2022, small enterprises by Q4 FY2023, and micro enterprises only marginally exceeded the baseline by Q1 FY2024. These patterns mirror the national evidence of Subramanian and Ranganathan (2023) and underline the regressive impact of the pandemic on the smallest firms.

Among coping strategies, 62.0 per cent of respondents reported drawing on owner savings, 41.4 per cent on informal borrowings from family and friends, 28.6 per cent on bank moratoria, and 17.4 per cent on ECLGS. The relatively low ECLGS uptake—despite Maharashtra’s above-average performance nationally—reflects the same awareness-to-utilisation gap documented for other schemes. Encouragingly, 47.4 per cent of respondents reported accelerating digital-payment adoption during the pandemic, and 31.5 per cent reported investing in e-commerce or B2B marketplace listing—a behavioural shift that appears to have improved resilience.

subsections.heading: 4.7 Digital and Green Finance Adoption
paragraphs: Digital-finance adoption, measured through a composite index of seven items, has a mean score of 3.24 on a five-point scale, indicating moderate adoption. As shown in Table 7, digital payment acceptance (UPI, POS) is near-universal (mean = 4.41), but digital lending platform use (mean = 2.86), cloud accounting software use (mean = 2.74) and GST-suvidha-provider use (mean = 2.91) lag substantially. Sector-wise, IT/ITeS MSMEs report the highest digital-finance adoption (mean = 4.02) and agri-allied MSMEs the lowest (mean = 2.61). On the green-finance front, only 14.3 per cent of respondents reported any awareness of ESG-linked lending products, and a mere 3.9 per cent had availed such finance, suggesting that the green-finance channel identified by Nair and Krishnan (2023) remains nascent in the Nashik context.

subsections.heading: 4.8 Inferential Statistics and Hypothesis Testing
paragraphs: The inferential analysis confirms several hypothesised relationships. First, the chi-square test indicates a significant association between enterprise size and overall risk-exposure category (χ² = 67.42, df = 4, p < 0.001), with micro enterprises concentrated in the ‘high-exposure’ category. Second, one-way ANOVA shows significant differences in mean overall risk-exposure scores across the seven sectors (F = 11.74, p < 0.001); post-hoc Tukey HSD tests indicate that the auto/engineering cluster scores significantly higher than IT/ITeS, food and beverages and other services. Third, multiple regression with perceived financial performance as the dependent variable and the five risk dimensions plus digital-finance adoption as independent variables yields a significant model (F = 78.43, p < 0.001, R² = 0.586). Credit risk (β = –0.34, p < 0.001), liquidity risk (β = –0.28, p < 0.001) and digital-finance adoption (β = +0.31, p < 0.001) emerge as the strongest predictors, jointly explaining 58.6 per cent of the variance. The negative coefficients on credit and liquidity risk confirm that these dimensions materially depress perceived performance, while the positive coefficient on digital-finance adoption indicates its resilience-building role.

Additional subgroup analyses sharpen these findings. A two-way ANOVA examining the joint effect of enterprise size and sector on overall risk exposure reveals significant main effects for both factors (size: F = 24.18, p < 0.001; sector: F = 8.43, p < 0.001) but a non-significant interaction (F = 1.32, p = 0.184), suggesting that the size gradient operates relatively uniformly across sectors. A mediation analysis using the Hayes PROCESS macro (Model 4) indicates that risk-management practices partially mediate the relationship between digital-finance adoption and perceived financial performance, with the indirect effect accounting for 38 per cent of the total effect. This mediation supports the theoretical argument that digital-finance adoption improves performance partly by enabling better risk-management practices, not merely by improving transactional efficiency.

Cluster-specific insights emerged from the qualitative responses. In the auto/engineering cluster, the dominant narrative was long receivables cycles (90–120 days from OEM buyers) combined with rising steel and copper input costs, with 71 per cent of cluster respondents reporting that they had drawn on owner savings in the preceding twelve months. In the wine cluster, export-oriented wineries cited exchange-rate volatility and shipping-cost spikes as the dominant risks, while domestic-focused wineries cited regulatory risk from inter-state excise differences. In the agriculture-allied cluster, perishability and price-discovery issues in onion and pomegranate markets drove liquidity stress, with limited recourse to warehouse-receipt financing. In the IT/ITeS cluster, by contrast, the dominant concern was client concentration risk, with several firms reporting more than 60 per cent of revenue from a single client. These qualitative insights reinforce the quantitative finding that risk profiles are cluster-specific and that policy responses should be calibrated accordingly.

body.heading: 5. Discussion
paragraphs: The findings presented in Section 4 confirm that Nashik District’s MSMEs operate within a financial-risk landscape dominated by credit and liquidity stress, with significant heterogeneity across enterprise size, sector and digital-readiness. This section interprets these findings in the light of the theoretical framework and prior empirical evidence, develops the study’s contribution to MSME-finance scholarship, and derives practical implications for Nashik’s MSME owners.

The dominance of credit risk (mean = 4.12) aligns with the information-asymmetry prediction of Stiglitz and Weiss (1981) and with the national-level findings of Singh (2022). What is distinctive about Nashik is the confluence of three reinforcing factors: a long receivables cycle in the auto/engineering cluster that depresses internal accruals; a collateral-heavy lending culture in regional rural banks and cooperative banks that serve the micro segment; and a documentation gap that prevents many micro enterprises from presenting GST-returns-based credit histories. The fact that 62.3 per cent of micro enterprises report a recent loan refusal—against 19.4 per cent of medium enterprises—quantifies the size gradient with unusual clarity and supports the case for size-differentiated policy instruments such as collateral-free limits calibrated to GST-returns turnover.

Liquidity risk emerges as the second-most acute dimension, driven by the same long-receivables dynamic but compounded by the low adoption of formal cash-flow forecasting (only 22.4 per cent). This is consistent with Sharma and Patel’s (2023) Gujarat finding that firms with formal forecasting routines had 23 per cent lower liquidity-risk scores. The Nashik evidence extends this finding by showing that the forecasting gap is itself explained by enterprise size, owner education and digital-finance adoption—a chain that points to a single integrated intervention: enabling MSMEs to adopt cloud-accounting and GST-suvidha platforms would simultaneously improve forecasting, build the credit-history paper trail and reduce documentation barriers to formal credit.

Market risk, while lower than credit and liquidity risk, deserves attention because of its rising trajectory. The 2022–23 commodity-price shock pushed raw-material price volatility to a mean score of 4.07, and the lack of hedging-tool adoption (only 28.1 per cent of firms use any hedging) leaves most firms exposed to downside shocks. The auto/engineering and chemical clusters are particularly exposed. Here, the resource-based view of Barney (1991) is instructive: hedging capability is a strategic resource that Indian MSMEs have historically under-developed. Cluster-level capacity-building—perhaps through the Nashik Industries Manufacturers’ Association (NIMA)—could address this gap through commodity-hedging workshops and bulk-procurement consortia that pool small-firm demand to negotiate better terms.

Operational risk is moderate but rising, driven primarily by skilled-labour shortage (mean = 3.81) and supply-chain disruption (mean = 3.49). The post-COVID rise in supply-chain risk is consistent with global evidence (Bruhn et al., 2023) and suggests that resilience-oriented supply-chain restructuring—nearshoring, dual sourcing, inventory buffers—is becoming a strategic necessity rather than an optional sophistication. Sandip University and other local institutions could play a direct role here by aligning their vocational and engineering curricula with the skill requirements of the Satpur–Ambad–Sinnar auto cluster, particularly in CNC machining, industrial automation and quality assurance.

Regulatory risk is the lowest-scored dimension but the GST-compliance burden on micro enterprises (mean = 3.71, with a 0.62 gap over medium enterprises) deserves specific attention. The finding that compliance costs are regressive is consistent with the broader literature on small-firm regulatory burden and supports calls for a simplified GST compliance regime for micro enterprises, perhaps through a turnover-based quarterly return with auto-populated inputs.

The awareness-to-utilisation gap in government schemes is one of the most policy-actionable findings of the study. Across all five major schemes, awareness exceeds utilisation by 30–55 percentage points, with the gap widest for CGTMSE (45.3 points) and CLCSS (34.6 points). The qualitative responses identify three recurring barriers—collateral, documentation and financial literacy—each of which is amenable to targeted intervention. CGTMSE process reform, perhaps through a digital-first application workflow with bank-side SLAs, would directly address the collateral and documentation barriers. District-level credit literacy drives, anchored by Sandip University and the DIC, would address the financial-literacy barrier. The fact that the Maharashtra Martand Udyog Shaskiya Yojana has only 38.0 per cent awareness underscores the need for a unified district-level scheme-information platform rather than the current fragmented outreach.

The COVID-19 impact analysis reinforces the regressive-pandemic narrative: micro enterprises contracted more sharply and recovered more slowly. The 47.4 per cent of firms that accelerated digital-payment adoption during the pandemic appear to have built lasting resilience, as evidenced by the positive regression coefficient of digital-finance adoption on perceived financial performance. This finding aligns with Subramanian and Ranganathan (2023) and Mehta and Agarwal (2024) and supports the case for digital-finance adoption as a core risk-management practice rather than an optional efficiency tool. The green-finance channel, by contrast, remains nascent—only 3.9 per cent of firms have availed ESG-linked finance—but the global trajectory suggests that this will become a more important channel over the next five years, particularly for the wine and agri-processing clusters that have natural ESG stories to tell.

From a theoretical standpoint, the study makes three contributions to the MSME-finance literature. First, it operationalises the Basel risk framework for non-financial small enterprises in an emerging-market context, demonstrating that the five-dimensional classification is empirically separable through factor analysis with satisfactory reliability. Second, it integrates the resource-based view with information-asymmetry theory, showing that risk-management capability (forecasting, hedging, digital adoption) materially moderates the relationship between risk exposure and firm performance—a moderation effect that the existing Indian literature has underexplored. Third, it extends the pecking-order framework to incorporate fintech-enabled formal credit as a hybrid between internal funds and traditional bank debt, an extension that reflects the post-pandemic structural shift in MSME finance.

The practical implications for Nashik’s MSME owners are concrete. A micro enterprise in the auto/engineering cluster that adopts digital accounting, registers for TReDS, and develops a simple cash-flow forecast can expect, on the basis of the regression coefficients, an improvement in perceived financial performance of approximately 0.7 standard deviations relative to a peer that does none of these. For a small enterprise in the wine cluster, the corresponding gain is smaller but still meaningful, reflecting the cluster’s higher digital-adoption baseline. The key insight is that risk management is not a luxury reserved for medium enterprises; it is a discretionary investment that pays off across size categories, provided the practices are adapted to the firm’s scale and digital readiness. Cluster-level collective action—through NIMA for engineering, through the Wine Park Association for the wine cluster, and through the District Industries Centre for cross-sectoral coordination—can lower the cost of these investments by pooling expertise and bargaining power.

Taken together, the discussion highlights three contributions of this study. First, it provides the first integrated five-dimensional financial-risk assessment for MSMEs in Nashik District, filling a district-level evidence gap. Second, it quantifies the awareness-to-utilisation gap for major government schemes with a precision that allows targeted policy design. Third, it demonstrates the resilience-building role of digital-finance adoption, a finding that has direct implications for the design of state-level MSME support programmes. The next section translates these contributions into actionable recommendations for stakeholders.

body.heading: 6. Recommendations and Policy Implications
paragraphs: On the basis of the empirical findings and the discussion in Section 5, this section offers targeted recommendations for five stakeholder groups: MSME owners, financial institutions, policymakers, academic institutions and industry associations. The recommendations are calibrated to the Nashik District context but several are generalisable to other tier-two industrial districts of Maharashtra.

For MSME owners, five actionable strategies emerge. First, formal cash-flow forecasting—even a simple monthly spreadsheet—should be adopted as a non-negotiable discipline; the evidence shows a 23 per cent liquidity-risk reduction associated with this practice. Second, the receivables cycle should be actively managed through early-payment discounts, factoring and the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS), particularly for auto-component suppliers. Third, digital-payment acceptance, cloud-accounting and GST-suvidha platforms should be integrated to build the credit-history paper trail that underpins collateral-free lending. Fourth, hedging instruments—even simple forward contracts on key raw materials—should be explored through banks or cluster-level consortia. Fifth, insurance coverage for business interruption, fire and key-person risk should be reviewed annually; the current 41.4 per cent coverage rate is sub-optimal.

For financial institutions, three recommendations apply. First, regional rural banks and cooperative banks should relax collateral requirements for loans up to Rs. 50 lakh where GST-returns data support the credit assessment, in line with the RBI’s recent guidance on cash-flow-based lending. Second, the CGTMSE application workflow should be digitised end-to-end, with bank-side service-level agreements of fifteen working days and a public dashboard of approval rates. Third, digital lending platforms should design working-capital products tailored to the receivables cycles of the auto/engineering and agri-processing clusters, perhaps using TReDS integration as a delivery vehicle.

For policymakers—the RBI, the Ministry of MSME and the Government of Maharashtra—five recommendations are proposed. First, CGTMSE process reform should be a near-term priority, with a digital-first application workflow, simplified documentation and bank-side SLAs. Second, MUDRA lending should be scaled up in Nashik District with a particular focus on micro enterprises, perhaps through a district-level KPI for loan officers. Third, the RBI’s priority-sector lending guidelines should explicitly recognise digital-lending-platform-originated MSME loans as priority-sector credit, removing a current disincentive. Fourth, digital-infrastructure investment—particularly last-mile broadband in the Sinnar and Niphad industrial estates—should be accelerated to underpin fintech adoption. Fifth, a unified district-level scheme-information platform should be created, perhaps anchored by the DIC in partnership with Sandip University, to consolidate the currently fragmented scheme-outreach efforts.

For Sandip University and other academic institutions, the recommendations centre on capacity-building. First, the School of Commerce and Management Studies should design a dedicated MSME credit-literacy and risk-management certificate programme, delivered in Marathi and English, targeted at first-generation micro-entrepreneurs. Second, faculty–student field projects should be structured to provide handholding support to MSMEs in preparing CGTMSE and CLCSS applications, with measurable impact metrics. Third, the university should establish an MSME Finance Research Cell that would conduct longitudinal tracking of the cohort surveyed in this study and provide annual district-level risk-monitoring reports to the DIC and the RBI. Fourth, vocational curricula should be aligned with the skill requirements of the Satpur–Ambad–Sinnar auto cluster, particularly in CNC machining, industrial automation and quality assurance.

For industry associations—particularly NIMA and the Nashik Grape Wine Park Association—the recommendations focus on collective-action mechanisms. First, bulk-procurement consortia for raw materials should be formed to pool small-firm demand and improve bargaining power. Second, cluster-level commodity-hedging workshops should be organised in partnership with banks. Third, a buyer-rating and prompt-payment disclosure mechanism should be developed to address the receivables-cycle problem at its source. Fourth, the associations should play an active role in the proposed district-level scheme-information platform, contributing their member-network reach.

body.heading: 7. Conclusion
paragraphs: This study set out to assess the financial-risk exposure and management strategies of MSMEs in Nashik District of Maharashtra, a strategically important but under-researched industrial region. Using a stratified random sample of 384 Udyam-registered MSMEs and a structured questionnaire of sixty items, the study measured risk exposure across five dimensions, examined risk-management practices, evaluated government-scheme awareness and utilisation, analysed the COVID-19 impact and recovery trajectory, and explored the emerging role of digital and green finance. The findings confirm that credit risk (mean = 4.12) and liquidity risk (mean = 3.94) dominate the perceived risk landscape, that risk-management practices are unevenly adopted, and that a substantial awareness-to-utilisation gap exists for all major government schemes. The regression analysis demonstrates that credit risk, liquidity risk and digital-finance adoption together explain 58.6 per cent of the variance in perceived financial performance, with digital-finance adoption emerging as a significant resilience-building factor.

All five research objectives have been met. The risk hierarchy is mapped, the management-practice gaps identified, the scheme-utilisation barriers quantified, the COVID-19 recovery trajectory documented and the policy recommendations developed. The originality of the study lies in its integrated five-dimensional approach, its district-level granularity for Nashik and its simultaneous treatment of post-COVID recovery and digital-finance adoption. The findings have direct practical implications for MSME owners, financial institutions, policymakers and academic institutions such as Sandip University.

Three limitations should be reiterated. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; a longitudinal extension would strengthen the evidence. Second, the perceived-financial-performance measure is self-reported. Third, the four-taluka sample under-represents the rural-interior MSME economy. Future research should pursue three directions: (i) a longitudinal study that tracks the present cohort for three to five years to capture the dynamics of risk exposure and management-practice adoption; (ii) comparative studies across industrially diverse districts of Maharashtra (Nashik, Aurangabad, Pune, Nagpur) to identify district-specific risk profiles and policy responses; and (iii) sector-specific deep dives, particularly on the auto/engineering cluster’s supply-chain resilience and the wine cluster’s export-risk and ESG-finance opportunities. Such extensions would consolidate the contribution of district-level MSME finance research to evidence-based policy in Maharashtra.

abstract: Purpose. This paper develops a conceptual framework that explicates how data-driven techniques deployed by digital learning platforms can support, scaffold, and strengthen self-regulated learning (SRL) among working professionals. As the half-life of professional knowledge shortens and lifelong learning becomes an economic imperative, working adults increasingly rely on digital platforms for upskilling, yet most SRL scholarship remains anchored in K-12 and university settings. The paper addresses this gap by mapping data-driven techniques onto the phases of SRL that are most salient for adult learners. Design/methodology/approach. The paper undertakes a conceptual review of literature published between 2000 and 2025 across Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. It synthesises four foundational SRL models (Zimmerman, Pintrich, Winne & Hadwin, and Boekaerts) with the contemporary literature on learning analytics, MOOC platforms, microlearning, and AI-driven personalisation for adult learners. Findings. The review yields a five-element framework that connects behavioural, assessment, social, biometric, and self-report data streams to learning analytics techniques (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive), and maps these onto the forethought, performance, and self- reflection phases of SRL. The framework demonstrates that data-driven techniques can substantially enhance adult SRL when designed with agentic, transparent, and contextualised principles, but risk reducing learner autonomy if deployed in a behaviourist, surveillance-driven manner. Originality/value. The paper’s principal contribution is an integrative framework that bridges SRL theory, learning analytics, and andragogical perspectives, with specific attention to the temporal, motivational, and contextual realities of working professionals. It offers actionable design implications for platform providers, learning and development functions, and individual learners, while flagging ethical risks of workplace learning analytics. Practical implications. Platform designers, employers, and individual professionals can use the framework to evaluate, design, and enact data-driven SRL supports that are both effective and ethically defensible.
