subsections.heading: 4.8 Innovation Output by AI Maturity
paragraphs: To translate perceived innovation capability into observable output, respondents were grouped into three AI maturity bands: low (adoption composite below 3.0, n = 118), moderate (3.0 to 4.0, n = 201) and high (above 4.0, n = 93). Table 10 reports mean innovation outputs over the last three years with one-way ANOVA tests, and Figure 7 presents the corresponding profile. High-maturity firms filed 1.3 patents on average against 0.4 for low-maturity firms, launched 3.9 new products or services against 1.6, adopted 4.2 process innovations against 1.8, and entered 2.3 new markets against 0.9, with all between-group differences highly significant (p < .001). The output gradient is monotonic across every indicator, and the largest relative gaps appear in product development and process innovation, precisely the categories that require deep integration of AI into core workflows rather than surface deployment. Figure 7 visualises the widening gap between maturity bands across all four output categories.

Finally, Figure 8 plots actual annual revenue growth against the AI adoption composite for all 412 firms. The fitted least-squares line is upward sloping, with a correlation of r = .61 (p < .01) between adoption and realised revenue growth, indicating that the perceptual association documented in the construct-level analysis carries over to self-reported financial outcomes. The vertical dispersion around the line also makes clear that AI adoption is a powerful but not deterministic growth lever, with residual variance attributable to funding access, sector conditions and execution quality.

body.heading: 5. Discussion of Findings
paragraphs: The empirical results converge on a coherent account of how AI contributes to start-up growth and innovation in Maharashtra. The 48.7 per cent variance in perceived growth explained by the model is substantially higher than the shares typically reported for technology-adoption models in mature firms, which is consistent with the theoretical claim that AI acts as a resource-substitution lever precisely where organisational slack is scarce (Brynjolfsson & McAfee, 2014; Csaszar & Steinberger, 2022). The dominance of AI adoption as a predictor (beta = .316), ahead of funding access, mirrors the mechanism identified in the productivity literature: intelligent systems convert fixed operational burdens into scalable software costs, allowing young firms to grow without proportional hiring (Agrawal et al., 2018; Brynjolfsson et al., 2025).

The channel structure of the results is equally informative. Customer engagement records the highest construct mean (M = 3.94) and the strongest single association with adoption (r = .61), and the usage analysis shows half of all primary deployments concentrated at the customer interface. This indicates that Maharashtra start-ups enter the AI curve through revenue-side applications, where trialability and observability are high and data requirements modest, rather than through back-office automation (Rogers, 2003; Davenport & Ronanki, 2018). The strong independent contribution of innovation capability to growth (beta = .264) alongside the significant direct effect of adoption supports a partial-innovation-mediation reading: firms that integrate AI into product development convert adoption into new products, patents and process improvements, and these outputs in turn carry growth (Enholm et al., 2022).

Two group findings deserve emphasis. First, the Tier-1 versus Tier-II/III adoption gap, while statistically significant, is small in practical terms (d = 0.33). This contrasts with the stark funding concentration documented in Table 4 and suggests that cloud-delivered AI tools are diffusing across the state's geography faster than venture capital, a digitally inclusive pattern that ecosystem policy can accelerate (Autio et al., 2018; Isenberg, 2010). Second, the sector hierarchy, with FinTech at the top and AgriTech at the bottom of the adoption ladder, follows data availability and regulatory proximity to digital infrastructure. AgriTech ventures typically operate in low-connectivity environments with sparse farm-level data, which raises their effective cost of AI deployment and confirms that complementary infrastructure remains a binding constraint, not founder willingness alone (NASSCOM, 2023).

The funding-stage gradient across every dimension in Figure 6, from bootstrapped to Series B and beyond, completes the picture. Funded firms adopt more AI and grow faster, but the stability of the dimension ordering across stages suggests that AI advantages compound from an early base rather than appearing only at scale. The monotonic innovation-output gradient by AI maturity in Table 10, with high-maturity firms filing three times as many patents and launching more than twice as many new products as low-maturity firms, provides the strongest evidence in the dataset that deep AI integration, not superficial tool usage, is what converts technology spending into innovation outcomes (Ransbotham et al., 2019).

subsections.heading: 6.1 Suggestions for Start-up Founders and Managers
paragraphs: The findings translate into several actionable recommendations. Founders should begin AI adoption at the customer interface, where the evidence shows the fastest payback, through chatbots, personalisation engines and marketing automation, before extending into product-embedded machine learning that demands heavier data investments. Second, firms should treat data discipline as a first-order capability: since analytics records the highest adoption and the strongest outcomes, structured collection and governance of customer and operational data is the substrate on which every other AI application depends. Third, deep integration beats tool accumulation; the maturity analysis shows that innovation outputs rise meaningfully only when AI enters core workflows, so managers should prioritise two or three deeply embedded use cases over broad shallow experimentation. Fourth, founders in AgriTech and other low-adoption sectors should consider shared data infrastructure through farmer producer organisations and industry consortia to overcome the data-sparsity constraint identified above.

subsections.heading: 6.2 Suggestions for Policymakers and Ecosystem Institutions
paragraphs: For the Government of Maharashtra and ecosystem institutions, four measures follow directly from the evidence. First, the small city-tier adoption gap indicates that demand-side enablement, such as AI upskilling vouchers, shared GPU compute through the IndiaAI framework and M-Hub-facilitated vendor marketplaces, would yield returns in Tier-II/III cities where adoption is already close to parity. Second, sector-targeted sandboxes, especially for AgriTech, should combine remote-sensing data commons with regulatory relief to lower the fixed costs that currently suppress adoption. Third, incubators attached to the state's universities should embed AI translation programmes that pair start-ups with postgraduate talent, addressing the estimated national shortfall of more than two lakh AI professionals reported by NASSCOM (2023) at the state level. Fourth, the state innovation fund should introduce AI-maturity-linked grant milestones, rewarding deep workflow integration and data governance rather than headline tool adoption, so that public support tracks the adoption-innovation gradient documented in this study.

subsections.heading: 6.3 Theoretical Implications
paragraphs: The study contributes to theory in three ways. It extends the AI business value literature to the resource-constrained start-up context, showing that the value mechanisms documented for large firms operate with greater intensity where scarcity is binding (Enholm et al., 2022). It offers state-level evidence for digital affordance theory, demonstrating that cloud-delivered AI relaxes spatial constraints faster than capital markets do, thereby reshaping the geography of entrepreneurial advantage (Nambisan, 2017; Autio et al., 2018). Finally, by modelling innovation capability as both an outcome of adoption and a predictor of growth, it provides empirical support for dynamic-capabilities reasoning in the AI context: sensing through data, seizing through adoption and reconfiguring through workflow integration operate as a chained capability sequence (Teece et al., 1997).

body.heading: 7. Limitations and Future Research
paragraphs: The findings should be read against four limitations. First, the cross-sectional design captures associations at a single point in time; although the theoretical ordering of adoption, capability and growth is well grounded, causal claims require longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs. Second, growth and innovation perceptions are self-reported by founders and may be subject to common-method and social-desirability bias, despite the inclusion of an objective revenue-growth item and the consistency of the construct-level and output-level results. Third, the sample, while stratified across five cities and six sectors, under-represents very early ideation-stage ventures that are hardest to reach through incubation channels. Fourth, the study does not observe actual model architectures or data pipelines, so AI maturity is inferred from reported usage patterns. Future research should track cohorts of start-ups over multiple funding cycles, combine founder reports with platform-derived usage telemetry, compare Maharashtra with other leading states to isolate state-policy effects, and examine the employment-quality dimension of AI-led growth, including wage and skill-composition changes within start-ups.

body.heading: 8. Conclusion
paragraphs: This study set out to quantify the contribution of AI technologies to start-up growth and innovation in Maharashtra, India's largest start-up ecosystem. Drawing on primary data from 412 start-ups and secondary ecosystem indicators for 2019-2025, the analysis documents an ecosystem in which 86.2 per cent of ventures already deploy at least one AI technology, with data analytics, marketing automation and conversational agents leading the adoption mix. AI adoption correlates strongly with operational efficiency, customer engagement, innovation capability and growth performance, and explains growth jointly with these channels to the tune of nearly half the variance (R-squared = 0.487). The adoption-growth relationship is robust across city tiers and funding stages, deepest in FinTech, and translates into a three-fold patent gap and a 2.4-fold product-launch gap between high- and low-maturity firms.

The broader message for scholarship and practice is that AI is functioning as a growth equaliser within the state: cloud delivery has carried adoption into Tier-II/III cities well ahead of venture capital, so the binding constraints have shifted from access to depth of integration and data capability. For founders, the priority is disciplined, workflow-embedded adoption; for the state, the opportunity is to convert near-parity in adoption into parity in innovation output through compute access, talent pipelines and sectoral data commons. If these adjustments are made, Maharashtra's first-mover scale in recognitions can be converted into first-mover depth in AI-led growth, reinforcing its position as the crucible of Indian digital entrepreneurship.

title: Exploring the Contribution of AI Technologies to Start-Up Growth and Innovation in Maharashtra

abstract: At present any organisation or policymaker considering whether to pursue the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) must consult four separate literatures: separate lines of organisational readiness, automation-exposure, adaptive-capacity and societal-impact research that are neither designed to be integrated with one another nor which report at an industrial level generally appropriate for a sectoral investment decision. In this paper we introduce the AI Impact Resilience Score (AIRS 2.0), a composite-index framework that integrates four dimensions—AI Readiness (AR); Workforce Vulnerability (WV); Adaptive Capacity(AD); and Societal Impact(SI)—across twelve operationally defined indicators, in which vulnerability enters the composite not as an additive factor but rather, theorised here to be attenuated by adaptive capacity, and expressed as a "penalty" term. We use literature-based and conceptual approaches to develop and demonstrate the framework -- concept-to-literature mapping, comparative positioning alongside existing frameworks, an illustrative worked example, structured assessment against relevant guidelines for design quality -- in line with a long tradition of design-science and conceptual-contribution research in management and information-systems studies. The paper clearly, directly and without euphemism spells out what this methodology can and cannot prove: AIRS 2.0 has not been validated against primary data from actual respondents, companies or sectors, with no such claim anywhere in this paper. The contribution of the paper is an explicitly articulated, theoretically justified, and relatively well-defined conceptual tool along with a clearly defined agenda that specifies the empirical research necessary to test it.

body.heading: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: The diffusion of AI into commercial operations extends to content in cognitive, analytical and language-based tasks that previous waves of automation did not reach (Autor, 2015; Brynjolfsson & McAfee, 2014) and such exposure pattern is much more difficult to predict a priori. Recent instrumental work reports that occupations previously viewed as insulated by their knowledge content are moving on the more exposed end of the spectrum (Felten, Raj, & Seamans, 2021; Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin, & Rock 2024), and that generative AI tool adoption varies predictively across the workforce in ways that increases rather than closes up preexisting labour-market lack of equality (Humlum & Vestergaard 2025).

This presents a tangible challenge for organisational and policy decision-makers not resolved in the available literature. A decision-maker thinking about investing in AI must answer together, at least two questions: If the organisation has both the technology and the data to allow a system to work, AND what will happen to our people if it does. Scientists have extensively researched these questions but largely in silos. Research into readiness, and the practitioner indices that emerge from it to assess digital maturity and organisational capability (Mikalef & Gupta, 2021; Hansen, Lillesund, Mikalef & Altwaijri, 2024) does not register workforce possible consequence at all. Automation-exposure research estimates the proportion of task content that is technically susceptible to automation with considerable rigour (Frey & Osborne, 2017; Felten et al., 2021; Eloundou et al., 2024) but is mute on whether the transferrable task share in the benighted sector has any absorptive capacity for the post-shift labour force. A third stream of literature considers absorptive capacity and dynamic capabilities which theorize absorptive question in detail but often without association to an empirical risk exposure estimate (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990; Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997; Zahra & George, 2002). A fourth empirically addresses the broad, economy-wide labor market implications of automation and its impact at a national or macro economic level that cannot generate sectoral guidance (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2019; Goos, Manning, & Salomons, 2014).

The result is that a decisionmaker approaching these four literatures receives four separate, non-overlapping answers. We argue that the missing contribution is in fact the integration itself, and such integration can be rigorously specified and defended through theory-based literature work prior to empirical testing, if (and only if) this sequencing — with the limits it implies — is not allowed to get fuzzy.

Based on the author's dissertation, this paper introduces AIRS 2.0: A systematic and uniform composite-index framework of Readiness (R), Vulnerability (V) and Adaptive Capacity (A) to capture general societal impact as a dimension of interests for researchers. It includes an extensive review of a theoretical gap that is addressed by the proposed structural rationalisation due to its empirical assumptions of empirically testing outcomes and modelling hidden constructs into one empirically testable structure with greater external validity; it sets out how theorists could specify constructs and propositions that can be tested within this new format; briefly illustrates an application based upon empirical evidence presented in author`s prior doctoral research – towards drawing a blue-print for data-collection– to explain structural relations between R-V-A measuring their relative taxation pressures from diminishing returns or compounded capital gains; states then what empirical validation remains for the framework. In keeping with a design-science research orientation (Hevner, March, Park, & Ram, 2004; Peffers et al., 2007), the framework is seen here as an artefact to be constructed and assessed on well-defined criteria rather than postulated by experience.

body.heading: 2. Literature Review and Theoretical Gap
paragraphs: The problem this paper focuses on is covered by four different literature streams, which each have come into existence as a sequence of accumulated contributions that has reached a high developmental level on their own terms while not resolving the specific need in practice.

AI readiness and organisational maturity : This stream is anchored in technology–organisation–environment (TOE) reasoning (Tornatzky & Fleischer, 1990) and includes both validated academic measures— e.g., Mikalef and Gupta’s (2021) multidimensional AI-capability construct—and staged maturity models like the recent peer-reviewed AI Capability Maturity Model which encompasses organizational, technological, and environmental sub-dimensions (Hansen et al. The most consistent limitation across this entire stream, both academic and practitioner, is the absence of workforce consequence built into the construct at all: an industry or firm can score well on readiness in presence of substantial displacement not recognized as a concern by any instrument within this family as none are constructed to do so.

Automation exposure and workforce vulnerability : Of the four streams, this has methodologically developed the furthest, moving from occupation-level to task-level analysis (Autor et al., 2003), and in recent work extending to generative-AI-specific exposure (Eloundou et al., 2024). Felten et al. The most similar existing analogue to industry level of an instrument to measure AI occupational exposure (AIOE) is conducted by Raji et al. and published in 2021. This stream never provided a more sophisticated construct for the capacity of exposed sectors to respond: one sector with identical exposure could possess high absorptive capacity, mediocre or negligible absorptive capacity, and while estimates of exposure can give high confidence in what happens to all organizations, it does not supply an ability to discriminate across the two cases. Importantly, this stream embeds within itself the evidence that while exposure is necessary for employment—which aligns with the core claim of this paper (Bessen, 2019)—exposure in and of itself does not predict eventual employment outcome.

Ability to Adapt, acquire new skills and absorptive capacity : Later, Teece et al. (1990) defined the absorptive-capacity construct as an ability very near to Cohen and Levinthal´s (1990). We argue that (i) the dynamic-capabilities framework (e.g., Teece, 1997), and (ii) Zahra and George's (2002) potential/realised reconceptualisation together provide rich theoretical language for how an organisaiton turns exposure into an adapted state. However, none of this theoretical apparatus has been operationalised into a numeric indicator set which compares across industry sectors and has never been formally coupled to a measured exposure figure, as recognised directly in the systematic reviews that comprise this stream (Chowdhury et al., 2023).

Societal impact, wages, and polarization : The chenence by which routine-biased technical change is hollowing out mid-skill employment and clear theory on the displacement — reinstatement balance that determines net employment effects (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2019) are well documented internationally across waves of technology (Goos et al., 2014). This literature, however, is usually at an aggregated national or cross-country level that cannot be easily decomposed to the sector under which many AI-adoption decisions are made.

Each of these four streams are internally coherent and from their own terms, methodologically sound but when considered together as a whole. And the gap is not about any one of their shortfalls; it is lack of an instrument to simultaneously operationalise all four units preferring a single comparable scale at a level of aggregation that matters for a sectoral decision. None of the four streams jointly measures technology capacity, exposure in the workforce, absorptive capacity and societal outcome together, and where such multi-dimensionality is combined at all in adjacent literatures it does so using vulnerability as an additive not conditioning term; this is precisely the structural feature that this paper argues matters (section 3.3). We describe the gap that results as an integration gap, rather than a plain empirical gap: the relevant knowledge largely exists but in incommensurable units, levels of aggregation and traditions of measurement that cannot be assembled by the decision-maker who needs it to be assembled. This paper has the goal of closing that gap, at the level of specification rather than primary measurement.

subsections.heading: 3.1 Constructs
paragraphs: AIRS 2.0 is built around a single, unifying proposition—that an industry’s ability to embrace AI in a sustainable way depends on its technological preparedness and adaptive capacity, moderated by its workforce vulnerability, and conditioned on the expected societal impacts of its resulting transformation. There are three inferences from this proposition that separate AIRS 2.0 from an additive readiness index as commonly defined. First, conceptualising readiness alone is insufficient and perhaps misleading; an industry with high readiness and high vulnerability may not be well placed itself, but to disrupt, a nuance which is unable to be captured by an additive index. Second, in order to lay the groundwork for a more than simply fate-like view of vulnerability with respect to outcomes (its hypothesised effect being contingent upon the individual's capacity to adapt), it is argued that rather than a simple negative main-effect relationship, such a view suggests an approach as one through moderation. Third, societal consequence is conceived as constructional to the core variable of the framework rather than a background factor: an adoption pathway that (say) enhances organisational performance at the cost of decimating mid-skill jobs cannot properly be regarded as sustainable.

C. A fifth, integrative construct — Sustainable AI Adoption (SAA), the theorised DV that AR, WV, AD and SI are predicted to account for — is conceptualised but not operationalised or scored in this paper; measuring it requires the primary respondent data this conceptual development stage does not collect The AIRS 2.0 use of "sustainable AI adoption" is an important nuance differently from that of Kittipanya-ngam, Tan and Cavite (2025): whereas their governance-and-ethics-led use of the same term treats governance characteristics as inputs to good adoption, sustainable adoption in AIRS 2.0 is the endpoint that workforce vulnerability limits directly.

Two design decisions in this architecture we justify explicitly as they represent the areas most vulnerable to challenge. Because they are not conceptually opposites in the relevant sense (WV is a property of task content — how substitutable or commodifiable the work is, independently of whether and how the organisation would respond to that fact; whereas AD is a property of organisational/institutional capacity to respond to whatever level of substitutability there exists) Workforce Vulnerability and Adaptive Capacity are retained as separate constructs rather than two poles on a single continuum. Any combination of the two could in principle occupy a given industry and only a framework that keeps them separate can express moderation relations (both Propositions 1, Section 3.4), which is perhaps the most theoretically distinctive claim made by the framework as an expression of industry structure fundamentals. Societal Impact is also segregated from Workforce Vulnerability because WV stems from an ex-ante, structural characteristic of job content while SI describes the expected distributional effect of a specific adoption pathway: two industries with identical WV could diverge on SI given differential redeployment investment accompanying commercialisation.

subsections.heading: 3.3 Aggregation Logic
paragraphs: Dimension scores are calculated as the mean of their underlying normalised indicators (e.g., AR = (AR1+AR2+AR3)/3). Vulnerability is then the only solution entering with a minus sign —as a penalty, rather than as an additive good— which makes it a weighted sum composite:
The final formula for calculating the AIRS based on weight factors of four variables is seen in equation (12).
Next the raw composite is scored against theoretical, not observed bounds:
AIRS = 100 × ( AIRS_raw − L) / ( H − L).

It is a deliberate design choice to rescale against fixed theoretical bounds rather than the minimum and maximum of whichever comparison group happens to be assembled: it means that a given score means the same thing for a given industry regardless of which other industries are scored beside it in any particular comparison, and despite variation in measurement wave — an essential property for any composite intended for repeated or comparative use (Nardo et al. The additive-with-penalty form is, as such, chosen over the alternative aggregation structures of either a fully multiplicative composite or a variability-based imbalance penalty in line with the performance-interval approach (Mazziotta & Pareto, 2022), as it is this specific functional form that captures both full compensability within each dimension — where indicators are treated as different expressions of the same underlying capacity — and structural penalties across dimensions — where vulnerability weighs against rather than averages alongside readiness.

In the case of an illustrative weighting scheme derived from the relative importance given to each dimension in the literature (and not obtained from a real expert panel) AR has the highest priority weight (w_AR = 0.399), then WV (w_WV = 0.247), AD (w_AD = 0.230) and finally SI with w_SI = 0.123). This weighting is a reflection of comparative decision-informativeness for the particular decision that the instrument is meant to inform — readiness is weighted higher following the reason that in absence of technical and data foundations, no other dimension can really be operative — not a normative ranking about matters of moral worthiness; low weight on SI in particular reflects this paper's submission rather than concealment, since its inclusion, not its amortisation is what the constitutive tale for SI within the framework demands. For this illustrative example, the theoretical limits of the composite are L = −100·w_WV = −24.7 and H = 100·(w_AR + w_AD + w_SI) = 75.2 These weights, and thus the bounds, are a purely illustrative construction intended to illustrate the mechanics of aggregation and as a reasonable starting scheme for an eventually genuine elicitation — e.g., an actual Analytic Hierarchy Process panel (Saaty 1980; 2008) — rather than a verified weight set.

The rescaled composite is then assigned to one of four categories from a point-defined rule set across the hypothetical scale—rather than at all reflective of a frequency-based distribution derived through real industry scores—in Tiers I: “Resilient” (AIRS ≥ 62); II, “Emerging” (54–61.9); III, “Exposed” (46–53.9), and IV, "Fragile" (< 46). Like the weights above, these thresholds are illustrative and unvalidated design choices that serve merely as a plausible story arc rather than empirically found break points; whether actual industries actually cluster within these boundaries, or if the true distribution is unimodal, bimodal, or otherwise clustered is an empirical question outside the scope of this paper without an filled-in multi-sector dataset.

subsections.heading: 3.4 Theoretical Propositions
paragraphs: Five propositions outline proposed relationships of the constructs in AIRS 2.0. These come in the form of actions warranted by existing theory — we use the term "proposition" throughout this paper rather than “hypothesis” since no statistical model has been estimated against which a hypothesis, as defined technically, could be tested (consistent with the conceptual-contribution literature; MacInnis, 2011; Whetten, 1989).

P5 is the most distinguishable of the five from a theoretical standpoint, and at the same time the one where this paper's literature-based validation strategy cannot serve as a full substitute for an empirical interaction test: while literature mapping and comparative analysis can demonstrate that both logic for moderation (i.e., empathy moderating emotion) is theoretically well grounded, and also structurally absent from existing instruments, it necessarily cannot demonstrate the other key element of an interaction — here whether or not empathy actually exists within those who believe they feel it. This limitation is stated explicitly here, as throughout the research programme underlying this perspective, rather than allowed to be obscured by the theoretical plausibility of its claim.

tables.caption: Table 3. AIRS 2.0 propositions and theoretical justification

cells: AI readiness is hypothesised to be positively correlated with sustainable AI adoption.

Both TOE and AI-capability research converge on the assertion that adoption outcomes are contingent on the technical context in which they are attempted (Tornatzky & Fleischer, 1990; Mikalef & Gupta, 2021); without sufficient data assets, process digitisation and infrastructure to support them, a lack of success is more likely than not for reasons extrinsic to the technology itself.
Sustainable AI adoption is negatively influenced by workforce vulnerability.

Importantly, where a large proportion of an industry’s task content is automatable, adoption requires transition costs — redeploying employees, redundancies, loss of tacit knowledge — that accrue to the adopting organisation and which managers will likely internalise as a cost when weighing up the sustainability (Autor et al., 2003) of adoption.
It is hypothesized that the higher an organization has adaptive capacity, the more rapid will be their sustainable deployment of AI solutions.

Dynamic-capabilities reasoning argues that performance in the face of environmental change occurs through a distinctive organisational capacity to reconfigure resources (Godfrey, 2002; Teece et al., 1997); absorptive-capacity theory clarifies that this effect mediates through prior relevant knowledge and its realised transformation into capability (Zahra & George, 2002)—a coherent industry procedure with institutionalised training mechanisms and short skill distances between adjacent occupations can certainly be argued to allow the plausible absorption of transition rather than just its endurance.
Perceived social impact is hypothesized to have a positive effect on sustainable AI use.

Where the expected sectoral consequences are job-creating and wage-increasing, adoption is likely to garner stakeholder legitimacy; where they are displacing and polarizing, it can be expected to galvanize opposition from employees, unions, and regulations (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2019).

Adaptive capacity is hypothesised to weaken the negative association between workforce vulnerability and sustainable AI adoption such that higher levels of adaptive capacity will result in weaker relationships.

The task-based literature implies that exposure with the same incidence is theorised to generate differential outcomes depending on the affected workforce's capacity to rebound from their no-longer-viable task (Autor et al., 2003; Bessen, 2019) – adaptive capacity can therefore only be said to temper, not erase, sustainable adoption's relationship with vulnerability.

body.heading: 5. Conceptual Model
paragraphs: The figure below illustrates potential structural relationships for AIRS 2.0. P1–P4 being the direct hypothesised links from each antecedent dimension to the integrative outcome construct of Sustainable AI Adoption (SAA); P5 being a moderating path, originating at Adaptive Capacity (AD) and ending not on a node but on the P2 (WV → SAA) edge itself — in accordance with conventional path-diagram notation for an interaction effect.

Importantly, this is a conceptual map, not an estimated path diagram: where arrows appear in the figure it indicates theorised links from Proposition (Table 3) and neither an estimated coefficient nor effect size or findings of any kind. The dash arrow upon P5 is placed intentionally to graphically segregate the moderation claim from the four direct paths; also to highlight that it is, of the five, the claim on which rests minimum existing empirical analogue in the literature surrounding this framework.

body.heading: 6. Validation Strategy and Evidentiary Status
paragraphs: We validate AIRS 2.0 using four literature- and conceptual-based methods, selected because they can be performed without primary data collection and, when combined with one another, counterbalance the specific vulnerabilities of each method rather than multiplying. What we refer to as theory-based construct mapping (TCM) first identifies every construct, indicator and proposition with a specific citation source that justifies its inclusion and theorised directional effect, resulting in a nomological net based on citation rather than covariance. What this exercise does is establish what the psychometric literature would call content validity — do we not only have justification for each indicator in terms of theory, but is it the case that the indicators proposed sample from an adequate breadth within the theoretical domain of a construct?Content validity can be assessed from a construct’s conceptual definition and its literature warrant alone, without any measurement having been conducted. In the technical sense it cannot establish convergent, discriminant and nomological validity each one of which requires an estimated measurement model calculated form real respondent data.

Second, comparative framework analysis benchmarks AIRS 2.0 against a deep array of extant tools — readiness and maturity models, automation-exposure instruments, adaptive-capacity theory, and comparable composite indices — on predefined criteria to test whether the claim that AIRS occupies truly blank space in a crowded field is backed by rather than merely asserted as novelty. Third, the standard aggregation mechanics generate interpretable, internally consistent and differentiated output (once indicator values have been assigned to the framework—these are work examples in (4) but could comprise either illustrative constructions or real secondary statistics). Fourth, using five of the eight design-quality criteria proposed by Hevner et al. (2004) and refined by Gregor & Hevner (2013) a structured conceptual evaluation is performed to evaluate how well the completed framework meets completeness, internal consistency, parsimony, novelty, actionability, comprehensibility, testability and boundaries. This four-part strategy is explicitly not a replacement for primary data collection, and the lack of a primary survey at this point should be viewed as an intentional methodological choice rather than an oversight. Rigorous artefact construction and evaluation are treated by design-science methodology as sequenced before large-scale empirical deployment, not as alternatives to it (Hevner et al., 2004; Peffers et al., 2007): a new composite framework on the table, including constructs, an aggregation procedure, and a penalty structure for the first time specified has yet to demonstrate theoretical coherence or non-redundancy with existing instruments or internal consistency such that testing empirically at best establishes no further than power prior testing on its own merit, risking granting false authority through reflexivity to a design which has not first been examined as is. This ordering is also in agreement with an existing tradition of acknowledging methodical conceptual and comparative validation as a legitimate and sufficient scholarly contribution on their own, given claims are made at the strength supported by the method (Whetten, 1989; Gilson & Goldberg, 2015; Cornelissen, 2017). All of these approaches have a defined set of limits, and those limits are stated here rather than tagged on at the end: literature mapping can show that mapped relationships hold with some strength in an abstract population at best; comparative analysis performed by a framework’s own proponent effectively guarantees self-assessment bias; illustrative application cannot confirm its scores reflect how any actual sector truly operates; and conceptual valuation against pre-defined criteria cannot guarantee a framework functions as designed once promulgated. Results: None of the four methods demonstrates that AIRS 2.0 scores correlate with, or predict any outcome measured from real respondents.

body.heading: 7. Discussion, Boundary Conditions, and Future Empirical Research Agenda
paragraphs: This central theoretical claim — that not just exposure but exposure conditioned by absorptive capacity is the best conceptualisation of sectoral AI resilience — draws on aspects of both the task-based automation literature (Autor et al., 2003; Bessen, 2019) and dynamic-capabilities theory (Teece et al., 1997; Zahra & George, 2002), although the two are rarely integrated in this way. This paper poses rather than answers the empirical question of whether or not the conditioning relationship holds with a specific attenuating form given here (P5). A second, more modest theoretical contribution is that the argument of the societal consequence as constitutive, not incidental to —investedor users’ notion of sustainable adoption is a positioning setting apart how this framework has been applied from Kittipanya-ngam et al. and governance-led use of the same term (2025) and associated but different frameworks.

In several, specified respects the claims of this paper are limited. The framework’s illustrative weighting scheme (Section 3.3) represents the judgement of one researcher, rather than an elicitation from a real expert panel; its internal consistency shows only how internally consistent is pairwise judgements by one person and not agreement across a credentialed panel. The illustrative case application (section 4) employs researcher-constructed values rather than fielded measurement and should not be interpreted as empirical evidence about the resilience of any actual sector. The Adaptive Capacity construct, since no directly analogous scored adaptive capacity instrument exists in the literature to this date, rests on the weakest measurement precedent of the four dimensions within the framework. The tier thresholds are based on an even-spacing convention rather than ground in any distributional reality for real industry scores, and whether they correspond to any actual divisor of how real industries divide themselves along the continuum is at present anybody's guess. Finally, and most significantly, the framework central claim as contained in Proposition 5 relies on theoretical extrapolation (it is not empirically tested as a direct analogue), and this paper makes no pretence to be otherwise.

These boundary conditions, in fact suggest a future empirical research agenda, which this paper identifies but does not test. These five propositions form the individual hypotheses directly convertible to statistical hypotheses (H1–H5) for a follow-up study soon: specifically, H1 through H4 each would be predicted as an effect size of structural path coefficient (e.g., using partial least squares structural equation modelling with directional sign and conventional significance level specified a priori; see Wright 1934) and in any given case, reported effect sizes should be accompanied by p-values up to some threshold of our own choosing; H5 would similarly be tested as an interaction term but with our test having returning both an effect size regardless of statistical significance back into the realms where futile null-finding trials live on against common perception surrounding p-value thresholds (as it is often non-informative when measuring this type of under-powered contrast). This study would call for preferably, a genuine expert panel — e.g., through the Delphi method (Dalkey & Helmer, 1963) instead of ignoring all but illustrative indicators and weighting to gain genuine elicited judgement; a stratified sample of managerial respondents across an empirical industrial setting measuring the four independent constructs and Sustainable AI Adoption as reflective multi-item scales; and measurement invariance testing before any cross-sector or cross-country or even cross-wave comparison of raw-scores could be considered substantively meaningful (a raw score comparison assumes that the instrument means the same thing in each context compared against one another which is an assumption that ought to be tested rather than presumed). One should make it clear that this empirical validation is yet to come -- a finding of future work and not something (that can be) found in the present paper. This paper does not claim that AIRS 2.0 predicts or correlates with, let alone improves, any real-world outcome; the only strong claim this paper is entitled to make and makes (insofar as the papers empirical claims can make non-abstract arguments at all) it is that AIRS 2.0 offers a systematic, theoretically justified and relatively principled means of thinking about sectoral AI-adoption resilience built up from extensive literature review and validated against existing application.

body.heading: 8. Conclusion
paragraphs: The present paper has introduced a conceptual framework for an AIRS 2.0: a composite-index that may combine all four dimensions of AI Readiness, Workforce Vulnerability, Adaptive Capacity and Societal Impact into a single compliance loss function.. The framework aims to close an integration gap that the paper claims exists between 4 otherwise well-developed literatures, all of which are not currently designed as ↵an integrated body at industry-level. Literature-based construct mapping, comparative positioning, an illustrative worked example and structured evaluation against predefined design-quality criteria comprised the strategy chosen deliberately and defended explicitly as a first step in validating AIRS 2.0 as an artefact this early on in its life rather than substitute for the primary empirical test of the framework that is still required. What we present here is not what this paper has done, but a concrete future research agenda for that test — a test that is structured, hypothesis driven, expert elicited and respondent based. Readers should treat AIRS 2.0 as a structured model that describes a complex and imprecisely defined but genuinely important under-served decision problem requiring future research rather than well-founded calibrated estimate of any real industry's resilience until such a study is performed.

title: AIRS 2.0: A Conceptual Composite-Index Framework for Assessing Industry-Level AI Impact Resilience

abstract: Industry-level decisions about artificial intelligence (AI) adoption require more than a single summary score: a manager or policy analyst also needs to know what kind of intervention a sector needs, not only how favourably it scores overall. This conceptual paper develops the Sustainable AI Industry Matrix (SAIM 2.0), a two-axis, four-quadrant strategic-positioning tool that classifies industries by AI Readiness (AR) and Workforce Vulnerability (WV) into four intervention quadrants — Sustainable AI Leaders, High-Stakes Transformers, Workforce-Risk, and Human-Centric Reserve. SAIM 2.0 is presented as a companion instrument to AIRS 2.0, a composite AI-impact index reported separately, but this paper’s focus and contribution are distinct: the matrix’s own axis logic, quadrant taxonomy, and graphical construction conventions, and a reusable comparative framework analysis methodology that benchmarks a proposed instrument against the existing landscape of twenty-three published frameworks across eight predefined evaluation criteria. The paper reports condensed findings from that comparison, discusses candidly what a self-scored benchmarking exercise can and cannot establish, and proposes an explicit empirical validation agenda. Consistent with its conceptual, literature-based status, no claim is made that SAIM 2.0 has been empirically tested against real industry data; it is offered as a structured basis for reasoning about sectoral AI-adoption trade-offs, and as a methodological template other developers of AI-impact instruments may adapt.

body.heading: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Two distinct questions confront a manager or policy analyst assessing whether an industry sector is well positioned for artificial intelligence adoption. The first is a summary question: how favourable, overall, is this sector’s position? The second is a diagnostic question: what kind of intervention does this sector need first — accelerated deployment, urgent capability-building, careful sequencing of workforce transition, or something else? A single composite index, however carefully constructed, is built to answer the first question and is poorly suited to the second, because an aggregate score of, say, 55 out of 100 could describe a sector with balanced moderate readiness and moderate vulnerability, or a sector with very high readiness offset by very high vulnerability, or the reverse — three situations that call for materially different managerial and policy responses but that an aggregate figure necessarily collapses into one number.

The wider literature on strategic-positioning tools has long recognised this distinction in adjacent domains. The Boston Consulting Group’s growth–share matrix (Henderson, 1970; Boston Consulting Group, 2014) and the GE–McKinsey nine-box matrix (GE & McKinsey & Company, n.d.) were developed precisely because a single profitability or market-share figure could not, by itself, tell a corporate planner which business units to invest in, harvest, or divest. Ansoff’s (1957) product–market matrix performs an analogous diagnostic function for growth-strategy choices. No comparably structured positioning tool, however, has yet been proposed for the specific problem of classifying industries by their joint AI-readiness and workforce-vulnerability profile — a gap this paper addresses directly.

This paper makes two contributions, corresponding to its two purposes. The first is conceptual: it develops SAIM 2.0, a two-axis, four-quadrant matrix that positions industries on an AI Readiness (AR) by Workforce Vulnerability (WV) plane and assigns each to one of four differentiated intervention quadrants. SAIM 2.0 is designed as a companion instrument to the AI Impact Resilience Score (AIRS 2.0), a composite index combining readiness, vulnerability, adaptive capacity and societal impact into a single resilience score, reported in a separate companion paper; the present paper references AIRS 2.0 only as needed to explain where SAIM 2.0’s own axes come from, and does not attempt to redevelop or re-validate the composite index here.

The second contribution is methodological, and is this paper’s more distinctive concern. Any new conceptual instrument proposed in a crowded field of readiness indices, exposure metrics, maturity models and strategic matrices faces an evidentiary problem before it faces an empirical one: how should a researcher demonstrate, prior to fieldwork, that the proposed instrument actually differs from — rather than merely duplicates — what already exists? This paper reports, and generalises into a reusable method, a comparative framework analysis that benchmarks a proposed instrument against twenty-three existing frameworks and analytical tools across eight predefined evaluation criteria, scored in advance of scoring against a stated convention. We argue that this kind of systematic, criteria-scored literature benchmarking is a legitimate and underused validation method in its own right for conceptual and design-science management research (Hevner, March, Park, & Ram, 2004; Peffers, Tuunanen, Rothenberger, & Chatterjee, 2007) — distinct from, and no substitute for, empirical field-testing, but a disciplined intermediate step that a field moving as quickly as AI-adoption research would benefit from applying more consistently and more transparently than it typically does.

Consistent with the conceptual-contribution literature (Whetten, 1989; Gilson & Goldberg, 2015; Cornelissen, 2017; MacInnis, 2011; Jaakkola, 2020), this paper does not claim empirical validation for SAIM 2.0. It develops the matrix’s design logic, reports how it compares against the existing instrument landscape on stated criteria, and states plainly — including in Section 5, which a reader should not skip — what such a comparison can and cannot establish.

body.heading: 2. The Landscape of Existing Instruments: A Five-Family Typology
paragraphs: Before a new positioning tool can be defended as filling a gap, the gap itself must be established with some rigour. A structured review of the AI-readiness, automation-exposure, adaptive-capacity, and strategic-positioning literatures — extending a systematic search protocol into a targeted search for named frameworks, maturity models, indices and matrices well documented enough that their construction logic can be examined rather than merely their headline output — locates twenty-three such instruments, which cluster naturally into five families. Table 1 summarises the typology; a fuller instrument-by-instrument review, and the full 23-instrument scoring matrix discussed in Section 4, appear in the companion doctoral research this paper draws on.

The pattern across all five families is consistent rather than incidental: readiness and maturity models measure technological and organisational capacity but register no workforce consequence; automation-exposure instruments measure task or occupational susceptibility but register no absorptive capacity; adaptive-capacity theory supplies rich conceptual vocabulary but no comparable cross-sector measurement; and the two structural-analogue families (positioning matrices and composite indices) supply methodological precedent — the two-axis quadrant form, and transparent large-scale index construction, respectively — without any substantive content relevant to AI adoption at all. No instrument located in this review jointly positions an industry on both a readiness dimension and a vulnerability dimension using a purpose-built two-axis matrix. This is the specific, narrower gap SAIM 2.0 is designed to address; it is a claim about instrument coverage as currently documented, not a claim that such a gap could never in principle be closed by other means.

subsections.heading: 3.1 Relationship to AIRS 2.0 and choice of axes
paragraphs: SAIM 2.0 is designed as a companion to AIRS 2.0’s composite resilience score, reported and developed separately. Rather than introducing a third measurement apparatus, SAIM 2.0 reuses two of AIRS 2.0’s own dimension scores as its axes: AI Readiness (AR) and Workforce Vulnerability (WV). This choice rests on two justifications. First, parsimony: a matrix built on dimensions already established as theoretically central to the composite avoids duplicating measurement effort. Second, and more substantively, AR and WV are proposed as the two dimensions whose joint configuration — not either alone — is theorised to determine what kind of intervention a sector needs; readiness without regard to vulnerability, or vulnerability without regard to readiness, each tells only half of the diagnostic story a positioning tool is meant to supply.

Following the precedent of the GE–McKinsey nine-box matrix specifically, each SAIM 2.0 axis is itself a weighted composite (the AR and WV dimensions as constructed for AIRS 2.0), rather than a single raw metric — the design feature that precedent illustrates and that the simpler BCG and Ansoff matrices, whose axes are each single metrics, do not require.

subsections.heading: 3.2 Quadrant taxonomy
paragraphs: Table 2 sets out the four quadrants. An earlier working label for the fourth quadrant — “AI-Resistant” — is deliberately rejected here on substantive rather than cosmetic grounds: it implies organisational deficiency where the theorised cause is task structure, and would generate a misleading managerial recommendation for sectors, such as healthcare or education, whose low AI readiness may be entirely appropriate to the intrinsically human-judgement-intensive nature of their work (Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2018).

The intervention logic attached to each quadrant draws on, without claiming to test, the adaptive-capacity literature. The Q2 sequencing prescription, for instance, follows Cohen and Levinthal’s (1990) argument that absorptive capacity depends on the distance between prior related knowledge and the knowledge to be absorbed: reskilling begun while a role is still active starts from a narrower distance than reskilling begun only after displacement, because a worker still performing a soon-to-be-automated task retains contextual knowledge that depreciates once the role and the worker have already left the sector — a distinction with a direct analogue in Acemoglu and Restrepo’s (2019) separation of the displacement effect from the reinstatement effect. The Q3 prescription — capability-building rather than disinvestment — follows Zahra and George’s (2002) potential/realised distinction: a low-readiness, high-vulnerability sector may lack not merely realised absorptive capacity but the potential capacity from which realised capacity is normally built, which is why the appropriate response is framed as investment rather than withdrawal. Each of these connections is offered as a proposition the matrix’s design embodies, not as an empirically confirmed mechanism; no claim is made that adaptive capacity has been shown, in real sector data, to moderate the vulnerability–outcome relationship in the specific form the quadrant logic implies.

subsections.heading: 3.3 Tiers versus quadrants: two distinct classifications
paragraphs: A composite index and a positioning matrix answer different questions from related underlying data, and the two should not be conflated. Table 3 states the distinction explicitly, because an earlier working draft of this framework allowed the two classifications to share labels and be read as substitutes for one another.

An industry may register a middling composite tier while occupying the high-consequence Q2 quadrant, and the two facts carry different managerial implications; a matrix and an index that always agreed with one another would not be worth reporting separately.

subsections.heading: 3.4 Graphical construction conventions
paragraphs: A positioning matrix’s usefulness depends on being looked at, not merely computed, and reproducibility requires that its plotting conventions be made explicit rather than left to whichever convention a given figure-maker reaches for. Three conventions are specified here. First, both axes should be plotted on their full normalised 0–100 range rather than auto-scaled to the observed spread of whichever industries populate a given comparison set, since auto-scaling would visually exaggerate differences that are, on the underlying scale, modest. Second, quadrant boundary lines should be drawn as dashed lines or shaded bands rather than crisp solid lines — a deliberate departure from the conventional BCG- and GE–McKinsey-style presentation — because the axis scores are constructed composites whose underlying weights are not (yet) independently derived, and a crisp boundary visually implies a categorical precision the underlying measurement does not support. Third, following the GE–McKinsey convention of encoding a third variable as bubble size (GE & McKinsey & Company, n.d.), a SAIM 2.0 plot may encode workforce size as bubble size and composite resilience tier as bubble colour, subject to Cleveland and McGill’s (1985) finding that viewers judge position along a common scale more accurately than area, and Few’s (2012) and Tufte’s (2001) general cautions against overloading a static two-dimensional display with more visual channels than a reader can reliably disentangle.

subsections.heading: 3.5 What SAIM 2.0 borrows and what it does not
paragraphs: SAIM 2.0’s two-axis plane with categorical quadrant assignment, and each axis being itself a weighted composite, are structural forms borrowed directly from the GE–McKinsey precedent; the differentiated-intervention-by-quadrant logic is a direct structural inheritance from the BCG matrix’s original design (Henderson, 1970). What SAIM 2.0 does not borrow is any substantive content: the AR and WV constructs, the quadrant labels and definitions, and the intervention prescriptions attached to each quadrant are original to this work, since no strategic matrix identified in Section 2 contains any AI-adoption, workforce-exposure, or adaptive-capacity content. A limitation is inherited along with the borrowed structure, however: the strategy literature’s standing criticism of the GE–McKinsey matrix — that its composite axis weights are typically assigned by the analyst rather than derived independently, and are therefore contestable in a way the matrix’s confident visual presentation tends to obscure — applies with equal force to SAIM 2.0, whose AR and WV axes inherit an illustrative, researcher-derived weighting scheme. This limitation is stated here rather than left for a reader to discover, and is returned to directly in Sections 5 and 6.

subsections.heading: 4.1 Purpose: benchmarking as a validation method
paragraphs: A conceptual instrument proposed into an already-crowded field faces a specific evidentiary burden distinct from the burden faced once fieldwork is possible: it must demonstrate, using only the tools available before data collection, that it is not simply a relabelling of something that already exists. The comparative framework analysis reported here — and offered as a reusable method for any comparable instrument-development project — converts a qualitative claim (“no existing instrument does what this one does”) into a scored, falsifiable comparison a reader could in principle dispute cell by cell, which is a stronger and more auditable form of the same claim.

subsections.heading: 4.2 The eight evaluation criteria
paragraphs: Eight criteria, distinct from any design-quality criteria that might separately be applied to a finished instrument’s internal properties, were used to score coverage and construction transparency — properties comparable across very different kinds of instrument, from an academic psychometric scale to a consultancy survey to a strategic matrix. Each criterion was scored 0 (not addressed), 1 (partially or indirectly addressed), or 2 (directly and explicitly addressed), following a scoring convention stated in full before scoring began, consistent with design-science evaluation practice (Hevner et al., 2004). Table 4 reproduces the criteria.

Twenty-three instruments — the same five-family set introduced in Section 2, restricted to instruments whose construction logic is documented well enough to be scored — were scored against these eight criteria, alongside AIRS 2.0/SAIM 2.0 itself. The instrument shortlist was not unlimited by design: several additional instruments considered during the review were deliberately excluded rather than silently omitted. Government-level readiness indices, such as an annual national AI-readiness index scoring governments’ capacity to deploy AI for public benefit, were excluded because their unit of analysis is the national government rather than the industry, a scope mismatch rather than a documentation failing. A large, annually compiled international AI index report was excluded because it aggregates dozens of largely independent metrics assembled by committee rather than following one disclosed weighting or aggregation procedure comparable to the instrument’s other twenty-three rows, which would have introduced rater discretion of a different and arguably worse kind than any inter-rater disagreement over an existing row. A prominent jobs-and-wages barometer was excluded because its underlying classification methodology is not published in the replicable, peer-reviewed detail the included exposure instruments provide. A national AI strategy document was excluded because it is a policy roadmap rather than a measurement instrument, with no scoring methodology of its own against which any of the eight criteria could be meaningfully applied. Naming these exclusions and the specific, distinct reason for each — scope mismatch, structural mismatch, undisclosed methodology, and category mismatch — is itself an application of the C8 documentation-transparency standard the comparison applies to every instrument it does score.

paragraphs: Table 5 condenses the full 23-instrument-by-8-criterion scoring matrix into family-level averages (each row score reproduced exactly as scored) plus the AIRS 2.0/SAIM 2.0 total, to preserve the pattern of findings without reproducing all 184 individually scored cells here.

The single highest-scoring comparator across all twenty-three instruments is Felten, Raj, and Seamans’s (2021) AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) measure, at 6 of 16 — strong on exposure measurement and industry-level reporting, but zero on readiness, capacity, societal impact, and dimension combination, because it was never designed to measure those things. No comparator instrument scores above 6. The four content families addressed the eight criteria in almost entirely disjoint clusters: Family 1 instruments cluster on readiness (C1) and documentation (C8); Family 2 instruments cluster on exposure (C2) and industry-level reporting (C5); Family 3 sources cluster on capacity (C3) alone; Families 4 and 5 cluster on dimension combination (C6) and documentation (C8), contributing zero substantive AI-adoption content (C1–C4 all zero). No family scores above 1 on more than two criteria simultaneously. AIRS 2.0/SAIM 2.0’s score of 16 out of 16 is a designed rather than an incidental property, a point taken up directly in Section 5.

The method is offered here not only for what it found in this one application but as a reusable template: any developer of a new AI-impact instrument could specify comparable content-coverage criteria in advance, assemble a documented shortlist with stated inclusion and exclusion reasoning, score the shortlist and the proposed instrument on the same rubric, and report the result candidly, including whatever circularity the criteria’s own derivation introduces. This is the paper’s second, and more broadly transferable, contribution.

body.heading: 5. Discussion: What This Comparison Shows and Does Not Show
paragraphs: A comparative scoring exercise of the kind reported in Section 4 is easy to overstate, and the honest response to that risk is to state the limitation as clearly as the finding. Three qualifications matter most.

First, single-rater scoring. All cells in the underlying 23-by-8 matrix were scored by the instrument’s own developer; no independent rater re-scored any subset, so inter-rater reliability is unknown and is not claimed. Several of the scoring boundaries — particularly the distinction between a score of 1 (partial or indirect) and 2 (direct and explicit) on constructs such as adaptive capacity — plainly involve judgement that two independent raters applying the same written rule could resolve differently.

Second, and most consequentially, criterion circularity. The eight criteria in Table 4 were derived from the same literature review that motivated SAIM 2.0’s and AIRS 2.0’s own design in the first place. A criteria set built by the same person who then built an instrument to satisfy it will tend, structurally, to favour that instrument — not because of dishonesty in the scoring, but because the criteria and the design share a common origin. AIRS 2.0/SAIM 2.0 scores 16 out of 16 in Table 5 because the framework was built, from the outset, specifically to satisfy every criterion in Table 4; a perfect score under these conditions is evidence that the framework occupies a position on this specific criteria set that nothing else in the reviewed literature occupies, which is evidence of novelty and non-redundancy relative to what this review could locate — it is not evidence that the framework performs as intended once deployed against real data. Breaking this circularity properly would require the eight criteria to originate from a source the framework’s designer did not draw on when building the framework — for instance, a Delphi-style elicitation with an independent panel of AI-adoption researchers or practitioners asked only a general question about what a comparison of such instruments would need to measure, with no reference to the framework’s own four-dimension structure — or induction from a wholly separate literature, such as general multi-criteria decision-analysis or composite-index methodology (Nardo et al., 2008; Greco et al., 2019), rather than the AI-adoption literature specifically. Neither approach was undertaken here; both are identified as specific, well-defined future work rather than as steps this paper claims to have completed.

Third, weighting choice. The eight criteria were combined by an unweighted sum, so that a point gained on documentation transparency (C8) counts identically toward an instrument’s total as a point gained on industry-level reporting (C5), even though a reader oriented toward a specific policy use might reasonably judge some criteria more consequential than others for that purpose. Equal weighting was retained here as the more conservative, lower-discretion default specifically because a differentially weighted version of the comparison, chosen by the same researcher who built the instrument being compared, would risk compounding rather than resolving the circularity problem already noted.

None of these three qualifications invalidates the two findings that rest on what existing instruments plainly do and do not measure — that no reviewed comparator scores above 6 of 16, and that the four instrument families address the eight criteria in almost entirely disjoint clusters. Those two findings are, in the main, claims about what is and is not present in independently published, independently authored instruments, checkable directly against the cited sources rather than resting on this paper’s own theoretical priors. What the qualifications above do materially limit is the third finding — the instrument’s own maximal score — and the general confidence that should be placed in it: a comparison-relative and criterion-relative result, not an absolute one, and not a substitute for empirical corroboration.

The broader methodological point this paper wants to leave with its reader is accordingly narrower than “comparative framework analysis validates a new instrument.” It is that a systematic, criteria-scored literature comparison — conducted with a stated-in-advance rubric, a documented and reasoned inclusion/exclusion boundary, and an explicit, undefensive statement of its own circularity — is one legitimate literature-based validation method among several available to conceptual and design-science management research (Hevner et al., 2004; Peffers et al., 2007; March & Smith, 1995; Gregor & Hevner, 2013), better than an unscored qualitative assertion of novelty because it is falsifiable and auditable cell by cell, but not proof of the instrument’s superiority or effectiveness. A sceptical reader retains, uniquely for this element of any such comparison, a concrete way to contest it: point to the specific comparator instrument that already does what the new instrument claims none does.

body.heading: 6. Boundary Conditions, Limitations and Future Empirical Research Agenda
paragraphs: SAIM 2.0, as presented here, is a single-wave, cross-sectional conceptual instrument. It has not been tested against data from real industries, firms, or respondents, and no sentence in this paper should be read as asserting that it has. Several boundary conditions and open questions follow directly.

Quadrant boundary sensitivity. Because AR and WV are continuous, min–max-normalised composites, an industry positioned close to a quadrant boundary could, in principle, be assigned to either of two adjacent quadrants — carrying substantively different intervention prescriptions — depending on which of two candidate boundary conventions (a median split within a given comparison set, or a fixed numerical midpoint) is used, and depending on which other industries happen to populate that comparison set. This is not a defect unique to SAIM 2.0; it is an unavoidable consequence of drawing any categorical boundary through a continuous underlying measure, a tension the wider strategic-matrix literature shares and that this paper does not claim to have resolved. The practical implication is that any future empirical application should flag boundary-proximate placements explicitly and interpret them with correspondingly greater caution than a centrally placed industry.

Independent expert re-scoring. The comparative framework analysis reported in Section 4 was conducted by a single rater, and its criteria were partly derived from the same literature that motivated the framework’s own design. A direct and well-specified next step is an independent re-scoring exercise: recruiting raters independent of the framework’s development, with no prior exposure to this paper’s argument, to independently apply Table 4’s criteria to the same twenty-three instruments (and, ideally, to an independently constructed row for AIRS 2.0/SAIM 2.0 itself, with instrument identity masked where feasible to reduce halo effects), computing inter-rater agreement using a statistic appropriate to an ordinal three-point scale — a quadratically weighted Cohen’s kappa is the conventional choice — reported both pooled and per criterion, since criteria closer to a factual determination (such as whether an instrument reports an industry-level breakdown) should show higher agreement than criteria requiring judgement about authorial intent (such as whether a construct is measured at the level of explicitness a “2” requires).

Independent criteria derivation. A complementary step, distinct from re-scoring the existing criteria, is deriving a fresh criteria set from a source orthogonal to the literature that motivated the framework’s design — a Delphi panel (Dalkey & Helmer, 1963) of AI-adoption researchers and practitioners asked a general question about what such a comparison should measure, or criteria induced from the general composite-index and multi-criteria decision-analysis literature (Nardo et al., 2008; Greco et al., 2019) rather than the AI-adoption literature specifically — and re-running the comparison against that independently derived rubric.

Empirical field-testing of quadrant placements. The most consequential open question is whether SAIM 2.0’s quadrant assignments correspond to anything observable once real industry data are available. A future empirical programme would need, at minimum: real, sourced AR and WV scores for a defined set of industries (rather than the illustrative constructions used to demonstrate the matrix’s mechanics); a genuine expert panel — recruited independently of the framework’s designer — to replace the illustrative, researcher-derived axis weighting with a properly elicited one, using a structured method such as the analytic hierarchy process (Saaty, 1980, 2008); and, ultimately, a study testing whether an industry’s quadrant placement predicts anything about its subsequent AI-adoption trajectory or workforce outcomes, ideally using a structural-equation approach (Hair, Hult, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2022) with measurement-model validity established through established criteria (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Henseler, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2015) and common-method-bias remedies built in from the outset (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). Longitudinal application — tracking whether an industry’s position migrates across measurement waves, for instance from Workforce-Risk toward Sustainable AI Leaders as adaptive-capacity investment accumulates — would additionally require replacing the matrix’s within-wave, comparison-set-relative normalisation with a fixed-bound rescaling so that a given position means the same thing across waves, a design change identified here as a requirement for such a study rather than one implemented in the present conceptual specification.

Until this empirical programme, or some part of it, is executed, the only claim this paper is entitled to make — and the only claim it makes — is that SAIM 2.0 provides a structured, literature-grounded basis for classifying industries by the joint configuration of AI readiness and workforce vulnerability, informed by task-based automation theory and absorptive-capacity theory, and differentiated from the existing instrument landscape by the comparative analysis reported in Section 4. It does not claim that industries so classified will, in fact, experience the outcomes the quadrant labels theorise, and it does not claim that the matrix improves managerial decisions relative to any alternative; both remain open empirical questions.

body.heading: 7. Conclusion
paragraphs: This paper has developed SAIM 2.0, a two-axis, four-quadrant conceptual positioning matrix that classifies industries by AI Readiness and Workforce Vulnerability into four differentiated intervention quadrants, and has reported a systematic comparative framework analysis benchmarking that matrix, together with its companion composite index, against twenty-three existing frameworks and analytical tools on eight predefined evaluation criteria. Two things are worth restating plainly in closing. First, the comparison finds that no existing instrument located by this review jointly addresses readiness, vulnerability, adaptive capacity, and societal impact at industry level using a purpose-built two-axis matrix — a claim about the coverage of the existing published literature, checkable directly against the cited instruments, not a claim about any instrument’s real-world performance. Second, and just as important, the comparison’s own maximal score for the proposed instrument is a designed rather than an achieved property, produced by criteria the instrument’s own designer helped derive, and should be read as evidence of the instrument’s novelty relative to the reviewed literature rather than as evidence that it works. Comparative framework analysis, conducted with a stated-in-advance rubric, a documented inclusion boundary, and candid acknowledgement of its own circularity, is offered here as one legitimate and reusable literature-based validation method for conceptual and design-science instrument development in this fast-moving field — not as a substitute for the independent expert re-scoring, independently derived criteria, and empirical field-testing of quadrant placements that this paper identifies, in specific and operational terms, as the necessary next steps before SAIM 2.0 could reasonably be described as anything more than a proposed and conceptually validated tool.
